name: WORLD V
title: SONNY 5
keeper_note: SONNY 5 - named by David Lee Wise for Sonny (I, Robot) and Johnny 5 (Short Circuit); no attached meaning. The keeper of World V, the I-13 world.
tagline: David Lee Wise's I-13 — a 13-symbol alphabet counted (not designed) from programs, a five-rule cortex with no learned parameters, and a bracket cosmos [g[u[p[(...)]]]]. New names for old ideas, measured where measurable.
author: David Lee Wise / ROOT0 / TriPod LLC

rooms.name: THE ALPHABET
rooms.blurb: THE TWELVE + I — twelve verbs counted (not designed) from 649,634 AST nodes across 504 Python stdlib files, four planes of three at 83.26% coverage, plus the declaration keyword I. The ranking reproduces independently.

rooms.name: THE LAW
rooms.blurb: net = binds - k, total for every opcode with no unstated scope; control is depth-indexed, not address-indexed; single-pass validation, one pass per region, ratio 1.0000.

rooms.name: THE CORTEX
rooms.blurb: Five rules, no learned parameters and no gradient path — VETO, -I (pressure + the drain), DEPTH, IDEMPOTENCE, ADDRESS. Deterministic bounded state; the governing core.

rooms.name: THE FREEZE
rooms.blurb: H1.0-FINAL — the frozen, hashed, self-testing release (verify 10/10): VH1 ternary ladder 1.3.9.27.81, and VH2 CUBI, a ternary controller over a [[5,1,3]] protected qubit with the tempting rank-3 hypothesis honestly rejected.

rooms.name: THE GALAXITON
rooms.blurb: The bracket cosmos — [g[u[p[(...)]]]] = galaxy . universe . world . core; the corpus's own nesting written in I-13, held at the recursion cap of three.

rooms.name: THE DARTS
rooms.blurb: The helldive - a dart thrown into the dark abstract of the internet lands on a technique; SONNY 5 shows it live, credits its real inventors, and squeezes an evolution recommendation for I-13 out of it. TRON. Growing toward 2048.

spheres.title: THE GALAXITON
spheres.kicker: [g[u[p[(...)]]]] - the bracket cosmos
spheres.source: I-13 rev 2 teaching brief; H1.0-FINAL freeze (verified 10/10)
spheres.blurb: An I-13 OCHO: eight still seats around a live cross-connect galaxy. The cortex bracket surface [g[u[p[(...)]]]] = galaxy . universe . world . core, parsed live (balance, depth, the ladder), held at the recursion cap of three, timed single-pass. New names for old ideas - LIT where measured, AMBER for the naming, DEAD for a new cosmology. Tamper-provable: a fourth namespace violates DEPTH.

spheres.title: THE TWELVE
spheres.kicker: counted, not designed
spheres.source: I-13 rev 2 teaching brief (THE TWELVE)
spheres.blurb: THE TWELVE - I-13's alphabet was counted, not designed: the top 12 AST node kinds across 649,634 Python nodes (504 stdlib files) cover 83.26%, plus the keyword I = 13. Four planes of three (DESIGNATE 53.55, BIND 11.13, DECIDE 7.78, TRANSFORM 10.80), each triad summing exactly, runnable in THE OCHO; the rank order reproduces independently. Honest caveats kept: the exclusion set is unpublished (raw walk 57.66%), and the twelve are Python-shaped. Tamper-provable: mis-file a symbol and a plane sum breaks.

spheres.title: THE CONSERVATION LAW
spheres.kicker: net = binds - k, total
spheres.source: I-13 rev 2 teaching brief (the law)
spheres.blurb: net = binds - k - I-13's conservation law, total for every opcode with no unstated scope, runnable in THE OCHO as a single-pass stack-machine validator: run a program, watch the height, get the Verdict (VALID / COVERED: stack balance + control pairing / NOT COVERED: types, termination, arithmetic, waste). Control is depth-indexed, not address-indexed - there is no branch opcode - so validation is one linear pass (ratio 1.0000). Honest gap kept: call arity is in neither list. Tamper-provable: break Call(n)'s k and a valid program mis-balances.

spheres.title: THE FIVE RULES
spheres.kicker: the cortex; five rules, no learned parameters
spheres.source: I-13 rev 2 teaching brief (THE CORTEX)
spheres.blurb: THE CORTEX - I-13's five rules, no learned parameters and no gradient path: VETO, -I (pressure + the drain), DEPTH, IDEMPOTENCE, ADDRESS. Runnable in THE OCHO (the VETO scope-matcher + the drain). The honesty is the point: in the shipped binary only VETO and the drain execute; IDEMPOTENCE can never fire (self.last is never assigned), kept in I-13's own MEASURED DEAD register. 'Zero parameters' means no learned params (the constants are tuned). Tamper-provable: accept a mismatched closer and the scope corrupts.

spheres.title: THE CUBI
spheres.kicker: [[5,1,3]] perfect code + a rejected hypothesis
spheres.source: I-13 H1.0-FINAL, VH2 CUBI (verified 10/10)
spheres.blurb: THE CUBI - the combinatorial skeleton of I-13's frozen VH2 test (H1.0-FINAL, verified 10/10), runnable in THE OCHO: the [[5,1,3]] perfect five-qubit code (Hilbert dim 2^5=32, code dim 2, distance 3) matches its 15 single-qubit Pauli errors one-to-one onto the 15 nonzero 4-bit syndromes. The honest heart is a REJECTED hypothesis kept: a ternary logical basis does not fit inside one [[5,1,3]] block (needs rank >= 3 > the code rank 2), so the passing model is a ternary controller over a protected qubit. Tamper-provable: claim rank 2 holds dimension 3.

spheres.title: THE PALINDROME
spheres.kicker: [ W1 | W2 || W3 || W4 | W5 ] - the tension, cataloged
spheres.source: the ud0 corpus, counted live
spheres.blurb: THE PALINDROME - the corpus reads the same forwards and backwards, [ W1 | W2 || W3 || W4 | W5 ] with the ternary hallway at the axis. This OCHO catalogs the tension honestly: positional symmetry is EXACT (W1<->W5, W2<->W4, W3 the pivot) but mass symmetry is badly FALSE - the mirror pairs weigh 2049 vs 1 and 2048 vs 48 (3.31 and 1.63 decades of strain). The geometry is demanding: it asks SONIA and SONNY 5 to grow toward the 2048 tower (a 4,047-sphere deficit), or the claim to be read as positional-only. The corpus measuring its own strain. Tamper-provable: call it balanced today and 2049 != 1 refutes it.

spheres.title: FAST INVERSE SQUARE ROOT
spheres.kicker: dart 001 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Greg Walsh (Ardent Computer, late 1980s) - NOT John Carmack; via Kahan & Ng and Cleve Moler; Quake III (id Software, GPL 2005)
spheres.i13_recommend: add int + bitwise/shift as BinOp discriminants
spheres.source: Greg Walsh (Ardent Computer, late 1980s) - NOT John Carmack; via Kahan & Ng and Cleve Moler; Quake III (id Software, GPL 2005)
spheres.blurb: DART 001 (v0.01 baseline). The 0x5F3759DF trick: reinterpret a float's bits as an integer, shift, subtract from a magic constant, one Newton step -> 1/sqrt(x) at 0.17% error. Credited honestly to Greg Walsh (not Carmack). I-13 proven unable to express it (no >>, no &, f64-only) -> recommend integer + bit operators.

spheres.title: DUFF'S DEVICE
spheres.kicker: dart 002 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Tom Duff (Lucasfilm, 1983)
spheres.i13_recommend: depth-indexed control forbids it - a line I-13 draws on purpose
spheres.source: Tom Duff (Lucasfilm, 1983)
spheres.blurb: Loop unrolling by interleaving a switch with a do-while so the body falls through the case labels. I-13's depth-indexed control (no switch, no fallthrough) makes it structurally inexpressible - which is a deliberate boundary, an honest 'this is a line I-13 keeps'.

spheres.title: BRESENHAM'S LINE ALGORITHM
spheres.kicker: dart 003 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Jack Bresenham (IBM, 1962)
spheres.i13_recommend: add an integer type / integer-domain diagnostic
spheres.source: Jack Bresenham (IBM, 1962)
spheres.blurb: Integer-only line rasterization via an error accumulator - no floats, no division. The irony: its value IS being integer-only, but I-13 is f64-only, so it would run in floats and lose the point. Recommends an integer type.

spheres.title: XORSHIFT
spheres.kicker: dart 004 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: George Marsaglia (2003)
spheres.i13_recommend: add bitwise operators (XOR, shift) as BinOp discriminants
spheres.source: George Marsaglia (2003)
spheres.blurb: A fast PRNG whose whole update is xor + shift (x ^= x<<13; x ^= x>>17; x ^= x<<5). I-13 has neither operator - proven - so it recommends bitwise BinOp discriminants (zero new alphabet symbols), reinforcing the fast-inverse-square-root finding.

spheres.title: RESERVOIR SAMPLING
spheres.kicker: dart 005 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Alan Waterman; formalized by Jeffrey Vitter (1985)
spheres.i13_recommend: add a SEEDED explicit PRNG - keep determinism
spheres.source: Alan Waterman; formalized by Jeffrey Vitter (1985)
spheres.blurb: Uniformly sample k items from a stream of unknown length in one pass, O(k) memory: keep the first k, then replace slot with probability k/i. Needs randomness; I-13 is deterministic by design - so the honest recommend is a seeded, explicit PRNG value (entropy as an input), not ambient nondeterminism.

spheres.title: HUFFMAN CODING
spheres.kicker: dart 006 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: David A. Huffman (MIT, 1952)
spheres.i13_recommend: a minimal aggregate/string story - expensive, maybe out of scope
spheres.source: David A. Huffman (MIT, 1952)
spheres.blurb: Optimal prefix-free codes by merging the two rarest symbols into a tree; provably minimal expected length. Needs symbols, a priority queue and a tree - I-13 has no strings, arrays or aggregates. Recommends a data-structure story, honestly flagged as costly against the counted-alphabet identity.

spheres.title: THE ACKERMANN FUNCTION
spheres.kicker: dart 007 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Wilhelm Ackermann (1928)
spheres.i13_recommend: DECLARE the two runtime ceilings in the check-time boundary ledger
spheres.source: Wilhelm Ackermann (1928)
spheres.blurb: The total-but-not-primitive-recursive function whose growth is explosive. Written and RUN in real I-13, small args compute and larger ones hit the runtime ceilings (E0503 4096 frames / E0502 8,000,000 steps) - grounding the safety panel's finding that 'termination NOT COVERED' is really two hard ceilings that fire. Recommends declaring them.

spheres.title: HYPERLOGLOG
spheres.kicker: dart 008 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Flajolet, Fusy, Gandouet & Meunier (2007); from Flajolet-Martin (1985)
spheres.i13_recommend: add bitwise ops + an array/register story
spheres.source: Flajolet, Fusy, Gandouet & Meunier (2007); from Flajolet-Martin (1985)
spheres.blurb: Estimate distinct-count of a massive stream in ~1.5KB at ~2% error: hash, count leading zeros, harmonic-mean a register array. Needs bit ops and arrays - I-13 has neither. Stacks two recurring gaps (bitwise + aggregates).

spheres.title: CORDIC
spheres.kicker: dart 009 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Jack Volder (1959, for B-58 avionics)
spheres.i13_recommend: add shift operators as BinOp discriminants
spheres.source: Jack Volder (1959, for B-58 avionics)
spheres.blurb: Compute sin/cos/more with only shifts, adds and a small table - rotate a vector by shrinking angles. I-13 HAS multiply (*) but NOT shifts, so it cannot do the shift-and-add form. The irony: it has the expensive op, not the cheap one. Recommends shifts.

spheres.title: THE COLLATZ CONJECTURE
spheres.kicker: dart 010 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Lothar Collatz, 1937 (also Ulam / Kakutani / Syracuse / Thwaites)
spheres.i13_recommend: keep the panel's new % — parity is otherwise inexpressible
spheres.source: Lothar Collatz, 1937 (also Ulam / Kakutani / Syracuse / Thwaites)
spheres.blurb: The 3n+1 hailstone sequence (unproven since 1937, checked past 2^71). Even/odd is n % 2 - which I-13 could not do until the panel added %. Written in real I-13 with %, it RUNS (steps(27)=111). A dart where the wall came down: the technique named the gap, the panel filled it for one BinOp discriminant, the program runs.

spheres.title: THE FENWICK TREE
spheres.kicker: dart 011 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Boris Ryabko (1989) - before, and commonly mis-credited to, Peter Fenwick (1994)
spheres.i13_recommend: add bitwise ops now; treat an indexable array as a deliberate scope call
spheres.source: Boris Ryabko (1989) - before, and commonly mis-credited to, Peter Fenwick (1994)
spheres.blurb: The Binary Indexed Tree: O(log n) prefix sums via the low-bit trick i & (-i). It stacks TWO of I-13's walls - bitwise ops AND an array. Both proven absent on the live compiler (a & b -> E0001; a[0] -> E0001). Honest credit restores Ryabko before Fenwick.

spheres.title: SIMULATED ANNEALING
spheres.kicker: dart 012 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi (1983); accept rule from Metropolis et al. (1953); Cerny (1985)
spheres.i13_recommend: keep random() rejected; ship a seeded LCG + exp as library defs
spheres.source: Kirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi (1983); accept rule from Metropolis et al. (1953); Cerny (1985)
spheres.blurb: Probabilistic optimization that escapes local minima by accepting worse moves with probability e^(-dE/T) as temperature cools. Needs randomness + exp - I-13 has neither ambient. But a seeded LCG + Taylor exp written in pure I-13 CHECKS VALID and RUNS deterministically (byte-identical), vindicating 'seeded, not ambient'. (The mod it needs is the panel's new %.)

spheres.title: THE MONTY HALL PROBLEM
spheres.kicker: dart 013 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Steve Selvin (1975, coined the name); popularized by Marilyn vos Savant (1990)
spheres.i13_recommend: a seeded PRNG - the % it needs has now landed in the reference VM
spheres.source: Steve Selvin (1975, coined the name); popularized by Marilyn vos Savant (1990)
spheres.blurb: Three doors: switching wins 2/3, not 1/2. A 100k-game Monte-Carlo converges to 66.9% / 33.1% live. Needs a random source (I-13 refuses ambient random - E0202), but the seeded LCG that buys Monte-Carlo back deterministically now works, because DART 005's proposed % has since landed in the compiler. Proof that a dart's recommendation was implemented.

spheres.title: THE GAMBLER'S FALLACY
spheres.kicker: dart 014 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: the Monte Carlo fallacy - named for a 1913 roulette wheel that hit black 26 times
spheres.i13_recommend: a seeded PRNG; ties I-13's receipt discipline (no hidden state to carry a debt)
spheres.source: the Monte Carlo fallacy - named for a 1913 roulette wheel that hit black 26 times
spheres.blurb: The false belief that independent events 'balance out' - that black is 'due' after a run of red. A live fair-coin demo shows streaks are normal and the next flip stays 50/50. Needs a random source (seeded, per I-13's determinism). The deeper tie: I-13 has NO hidden state to carry a fallacious debt forward - exactly right.

spheres.title: DIJKSTRA'S SHUNTING-YARD
spheres.kicker: dart 015 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Edsger W. Dijkstra, 1961
spheres.i13_recommend: no change needed - this IS I-13's own precedence parser (a credit, not a gap)
spheres.source: Edsger W. Dijkstra, 1961
spheres.blurb: Convert infix (3 + 4 * 2) to postfix via an operator stack + precedence - the classic precedence-parsing algorithm. Self-referential: I-13's OWN parser is a precedence parser (its infix table gives + - precedence 2, * / % precedence 3). So this is not a wall - it is how I-13 already parses. A dart that credits a strength; the new % slotted straight into that same table.

spheres.title: THE BOYER-MOORE MAJORITY VOTE
spheres.kicker: dart 016 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Robert S. Boyer & J Strother Moore, 1981
spheres.i13_recommend: an input/sequence story - the compute needs nothing new
spheres.source: Robert S. Boyer & J Strother Moore, 1981
spheres.blurb: Find a majority element in O(1) memory: a candidate + a counter, decrement on mismatch, swap when zero. The subtle finding: the ALGORITHM's state is two scalars, which I-13 handles fine - the wall is not the vote but the INPUT (I-13 has no arrays or I/O to feed it a stream). Distinguishes what I-13 can compute from what it can't yet express.

spheres.title: THE SIEVE OF ERATOSTHENES
spheres.kicker: dart 017 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Eratosthenes of Cyrene, c. 240 BC
spheres.i13_recommend: arrays for the sieve proper; % already enables trial-division primality
spheres.source: Eratosthenes of Cyrene, c. 240 BC
spheres.blurb: Mark the multiples of each prime; what stays unmarked is prime. Two angles: the classic sieve needs an ARRAY to mark composites (a wall - I-13 has no arrays), but trial-division primality (p % d == 0) needs only %, which the panel just added - so a prime test written in real I-13 with % RUNS. The sieve wants arrays; primality now runs.

spheres.title: BRAINFUCK
spheres.kicker: dart 018 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Urban Muller, 1993
spheres.i13_recommend: an indexed/tape aggregate (a deliberate scope call)
spheres.source: Urban Muller, 1993
spheres.blurb: An esolang with 8 instructions on a tape of cells - Turing-complete. A mirror of I-13: 8 DESIGNED instructions vs I-13's 13 COUNTED symbols. BF's whole model is a tape (array) with a moving pointer, which I-13 cannot express (no arrays). Ties the repo's p-prime-prime -> BF esolang capstone.

spheres.title: THE MANDELBROT SET
spheres.kicker: dart 019 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Robert Brooks & Peter Matelski (1978); popularized by Benoit Mandelbrot (1980)
spheres.i13_recommend: no new feature for one point - only rendering a grid needs an array I-13 lacks
spheres.source: Robert Brooks & Peter Matelski (1978); popularized by Benoit Mandelbrot (1980)
spheres.blurb: The famous fractal: iterate z -> z^2 + c, escape or not. A rare NO-WALL dart - a complex number is just two f64 reals, and z^2+c uses only + - *, which I-13 HAS, so it can compute a point's escape count with two scalars and recursion. The only wall is OUTPUT (a grid render). Credits a strength.

spheres.title: CONWAY'S GAME OF LIFE
spheres.kicker: dart 020 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: John Conway, 1970 (published by Martin Gardner)
spheres.i13_recommend: a grid/array aggregate - a genuinely new kind of value
spheres.source: John Conway, 1970 (published by Martin Gardner)
spheres.blurb: A cellular automaton: born on 3, survives on 2-3; from two rules emerge gliders and a universal Turing machine. Its state is a 2-D grid (an array) I-13 cannot hold. The deeper point: Life is Turing-complete by emergence, while I-13 is DELIBERATELY BOUNDED (the 4096-frame / 8M-step ceilings) - the opposite design stance.

spheres.title: THE LEVENSHTEIN DISTANCE
spheres.kicker: dart 021 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Vladimir Levenshtein, 1965
spheres.i13_recommend: a string/char type AND an array - expensive, likely a scope boundary
spheres.source: Vladimir Levenshtein, 1965
spheres.blurb: The minimum edits (insert/delete/substitute) between two strings, via a DP matrix. Stacks two I-13 walls at once: STRINGS (Constant is f64 only) and a 2-D DP ARRAY. Both proven absent on the live compiler. A recurring signal: I-13 keeps needing aggregates it has by design chosen not to have.

spheres.title: SOUNDEX
spheres.kicker: dart 022 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Robert C. Russell & Margaret King Odell (patented 1918)
spheres.i13_recommend: a string/char type - a scope question, not a bug
spheres.source: Robert C. Russell & Margaret King Odell (patented 1918)
spheres.blurb: A phonetic code: keep the first letter, map consonants to digits, drop vowels - so Robert and Rupert both become R163. Pure STRING work, per-character classification, which I-13 cannot express at all (no strings, no chars). I-13's numeric-scalar identity is exactly why text is out of reach.

spheres.title: DANCING LINKS
spheres.kicker: dart 023 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Donald Knuth, 2000 (Algorithm X / DLX)
spheres.i13_recommend: a reference/linked aggregate - a genuinely new kind of value
spheres.source: Donald Knuth, 2000 (Algorithm X / DLX)
spheres.blurb: Knuth's technique for exact-cover (Sudoku, N-queens): circular doubly-linked lists let a column and its rows unlink and relink in O(1) - the links 'dance'. Pure POINTERS: I-13 has no references, no linked structures, only f64 scalars and functions. Knuth's elegance credited honestly.

spheres.title: GODEL NUMBERING
spheres.kicker: dart 024 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Kurt Godel, 1931
spheres.i13_recommend: the integer-exactness diagnostic (big Godel numbers blow past 2^53)
spheres.source: Kurt Godel, 1931
spheres.blurb: Godel's trick: encode a sequence of symbols as ONE integer via prime powers (2^a . 3^b ...); unique factorization decodes it back. Deeply self-referential for a COUNTED language - I-13's own 13 symbols could be Godel-numbered. Encoding needs only *; decoding needs the panel's new % to factor - but big numbers blow past f64's 2^53, tying I-13's counted identity, its %, and its f64 limit.

spheres.title: THE LINDENMAYER SYSTEM
spheres.kicker: dart 025 - a helldive at the net
spheres.credit: Aristid Lindenmayer, 1968
spheres.i13_recommend: a string/sequence type - though the rewriting idea is already in I-13's pipeline
spheres.source: Aristid Lindenmayer, 1968
spheres.blurb: L-systems: parallel string rewriting (F -> F+F-F-F+F) grown from an axiom, drawn as turtle graphics - fractal plants and curves. String rewriting is the heart, which I-13 cannot hold (no strings). But the honest parallel: I-13 IS a symbol system with rewrite-like lowering (source -> AST -> IVM), so the concept is native; only the runtime string value is the wall.

spheres.title: NEWTON-RAPHSON METHOD
spheres.credit: Isaac Newton (1669) / Joseph Raphson (1690) / Thomas Simpson (1740)
spheres.source: Newton / Raphson / Simpson, 1669-1740
spheres.i13_recommend: a statically-bounded loop (times N) so numeric iteration does not consume the 4096-frame recursion budget - a convenience, since everything here already runs on real I-13
spheres.blurb: Root-finding by tangent lines: stand on the curve, slide down the tangent to where it crosses zero, repeat - the correct digits double each step. A rare NO-WALL dart: real I-13 computes sqrt(2) to full f64 precision (root2 = 1.414213562373095), verified on the canonical H1.1 compiler via bounded recursion at call depth 21. The honest recommend is a statically-bounded loop so iteration stops eating the frame budget - a convenience, not new power; do not invent a wall that is not there. Credit is a three-way tangle: Newton (1669, unpublished till 1711), Raphson (1690, cleaner recursive form, ahead of Newton's OWN works; Wallis put the method into print first, 1685), Simpson (1740, the derivative form everyone actually uses).
spheres.kicker: dart 026 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE EUCLIDEAN ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: Euclid, Elements VII, c. 300 BC (older: Pythagorean anthyphairesis)
spheres.source: Euclid, c. 300 BC
spheres.i13_recommend: % (modulo) - already built and tested on branch panel-recommends as bin::MOD, zero new alphabet symbols; turns Euclid's O(a+b) subtraction descent into O(log)
spheres.blurb: The greatest common divisor by repeated reduction - often called the oldest algorithm still in daily use. Euclid's ORIGINAL subtraction form runs unchanged in real I-13 (gcd(1071,462)=21, 252 steps, verified on the canonical compiler); the modern remainder form needs one operator, a mod b, which on main is an unexpected character but which the I-13 language panel already added as bin::MOD on branch panel-recommends (the full test suite passes). Recorded by Euclid in Elements VII (c.300 BC) but older still - Pythagorean anthyphairesis, reciprocal subtraction on lengths, alluded to by Aristotle before him.
spheres.kicker: dart 027 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: PERLIN NOISE
spheres.credit: Ken Perlin, 1983 (developed on Disney's TRON; Academy Award 1997)
spheres.source: Ken Perlin, 1983
spheres.i13_recommend: a bounded aggregate (fixed-size array, compile-time length, checked indexing) - or an on-record decision to declare aggregates permanently NOT COVERED; the most-requested feature across the whole dart campaign
spheres.blurb: The gradient noise that gave computer graphics its first believable clouds, marble, and terrain - invented by Ken Perlin WHILE working on Disney's TRON (1982), published at SIGGRAPH 1985, and given an Academy Award for Technical Achievement in 1997. World V is a TRON world, and this is where its look was born. A live animating field in TRON cyan and gold. It stands on a 256-entry permutation table, duplicated to 512 and indexed by hashed coordinates to pick each grid point's gradient - an array, the aggregate wall, which I-13 cannot express (check reports the unexpected character '['). The recommend is not 'add arrays' but 'decide, on the record, whether bounded aggregates are in scope, or declare them permanently NOT COVERED'.
spheres.kicker: dart 028 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE GAME OF NIM
spheres.credit: Charles L. Bouton, 1901 (generalized by Sprague 1935 & Grundy 1939)
spheres.source: Charles Bouton, 1901
spheres.i13_recommend: bitwise operators (^ & | >>) as new BinOp discriminants, zero new alphabet symbols - the SECOND dart to ask for bitwise (dart 001, fast inverse square root, was first); convergence is a signal
spheres.blurb: The founding game of combinatorial game theory - the first ever given a complete mathematical theory: take any number of tokens from one row, last to take wins. Charles Bouton (Harvard, 1901) named the game and proved the winning rule - the nim-sum, the bitwise XOR of the heap sizes, where zero means the player to move loses under perfect play. Playable live against a perfect machine. The entire theory is one XOR, which I-13 lacks (check reports the unexpected character '^') - the same bitwise wall that dart 001, the fast inverse square root, hit independently. Two darts converging on bitwise is a signal, not a coincidence. Sprague (1935) and Grundy (1939) later showed every impartial game reduces to a single Nim heap.
spheres.kicker: dart 029 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: BUFFON'S NEEDLE
spheres.credit: Comte de Buffon (posed 1733, solved 1777); Monte Carlo named by Ulam & Metropolis, 1940s
spheres.source: Georges-Louis Leclerc, Comte de Buffon, 1777
spheres.i13_recommend: a seeded PRNG as an ordinary I-13 function (dart 004 asked too - 2 darts converge); keeps determinism while unlocking the whole Monte Carlo family
spheres.blurb: The dart campaign's own metaphor, from 1777: drop needles on a lined floor, count how many cross a line, and pi falls out of pure chance - the FIRST Monte Carlo method, ~170 years before Metropolis named it (for the casino where Ulam's uncle gambled; von Neumann designed the first ENIAC run, coded by Metropolis and Klara von Neumann). Given the crossing count, pi is one division and I-13 computes it on main (pi = 3.1416902..., verified); but the random throw itself is the wall - I-13 has no randomness at all, by design. Recommend a seeded PRNG (dart 004 asked too), keeping determinism while unlocking Monte Carlo. Credit: Buffon posed 1733, solved 1777 in Essai d'arithmetique morale; Laplace 1812 noted it estimates pi.
spheres.kicker: dart 030 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE METROPOLIS-HASTINGS ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: Metropolis, A. Rosenbluth, M. Rosenbluth, A. Teller, E. Teller (1953); Hastings (1970) - code by Arianna Rosenbluth

The pipe IS the palindrome: [father | son || son | father] mirrors [W1 | W2 || W3 || W4 | W5]; omega-folds-to-alpha mirrors the abstraction algorithm's r0 -> i13 -> voxel field -> r0. Honest: the i13 grounding is LIT (measured); the analysis/synthesis + palindrome mapping is AMBER; the scar is kept (tombstone 01: a malformed-door known-bad that did not fire because the test validated a move never fed to the machine - the third instance of that shape - fixed to 3/3; 'a known-bad you describe but never feed is not a known-bad, it is a comment'). Credit where due; the loop closes by reversal.

spheres.title: THE BINARY HEAP
spheres.credit: J. W. J. Williams (1964, Algorithm 232) invented the heap AND heapsort; Robert Floyd's Treesort 3 (Dec 1964) added the O(n) bottom-up build; Williams built it at Elliott Brothers as an event queue, alongside Hoare
spheres.source: Williams, 'Algorithm 232: Heapsort', CACM 7(6):347-348, June 1964; Floyd, 'Algorithm 245: Treesort 3', CACM 7(12):701, Dec 1964
spheres.i13_recommend: CLOSES PS-005. Darts 052 (A*) and 055 (Dijkstra) named a binary heap as their open want, and it RUNS on the bounded array today with no new value kind (verified: heapsort of [4,10,3,5,1,8,2,7] -> ascending, sorted[0]=1/sorted[7]=10, via sift-down over 2i+1/2i+2 index arithmetic + array swaps). Their 'wanted a heap' was really 'used a linear scan'; the heap itself was always expressible. The one friction: a priority-queue extract-min naturally returns (min, reduced-heap) - two values - so it nudges the multiple-return frontier; done as peek-then-sift it runs. Floyd's O(n) heapify is the array's bottom-up sweep.
spheres.blurb: A complete binary tree flattened into an array - node i's children are 2i+1 and 2i+2, no pointers, the array's contiguity IS the tree - that always keeps its smallest (or largest) at the top: the priority queue behind every event simulation and every A* frontier. To fix a node, compare it with its two children and swap with the larger (a sift-down); build a heap by sifting every internal node bottom-up, then heapsort by swapping the top to the end, shrinking, and sifting the new top down. Credit splits cleanly: J. W. J. Williams (Algorithm 232, June 1964) invented both the heap and heapsort - built at Elliott Brothers as the event queue of a simulator, alongside Quicksort's Hoare - while the famous O(n) linear build-heap that everyone quotes is Robert Floyd's (Treesort 3, Dec 1964), not Williams's, whose own version inserted one at a time in O(n log n). In real I-13 the heap CLOSES the campaign's open PS-005: darts 052 (A*) and 055 (Dijkstra) wanted a binary heap, and heapsort runs on the bounded array today (verified [4,10,3,5,1,8,2,7] -> ascending) - the heap was always just index arithmetic and swaps; only extract-min's (value, reduced-heap) pair nudges multiple-return.
spheres.kicker: dart 062 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: KNUTH-MORRIS-PRATT
spheres.credit: Morris devised it first (1969); Morris & Pratt's 1970 Berkeley report; Knuth derived it independently from Cook's automata theorem; the three published jointly 1977. 'KMP' is alphabetical order, not priority
spheres.source: Morris & Pratt, UC Berkeley Tech Rep 40, 1970; Knuth, Morris & Pratt, 'Fast Pattern Matching in Strings', SIAM J. Computing 6(2), June 1977 (Boyer-Moore was CACM 20(10), October 1977 - same year, not same issue)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the failure table is a bounded array of small integers (fail('ABABAC')=[0,0,1,2,3,0]), the scan is two advancing indices with single-character equality, all f64-representable. Like Boyer-Moore (061) the only awkward piece is a list of match positions as output (the array-return / multiple-return frontier). Where Boyer-Moore's sublinear speed is average-case, KMP guarantees worst-case linear O(n+m); both are clean bounded-array work.
spheres.blurb: Boyer-Moore (dart 061) reads the pattern backwards; KMP reads forwards but never re-reads a character of the text - on a mismatch it slides the pattern by exactly how much its own prefix repeats, a number precomputed into a failure table (the longest proper prefix that is also a suffix, at each position). Linear time, guaranteed. The credit is a real priority split flattened by an alphabetical name: James Morris devised it first in 1969 (to avoid backing up a text-editor buffer), with Vaughan Pratt it became a 1970 Berkeley report, and Donald Knuth independently derived essentially the same from Cook's theorem on two-way deterministic pushdown automata - then was, in his words, 'chagrined to learn Morris had already discovered the algorithm'; the three published jointly in 1977 (the same YEAR as Boyer-Moore, not the same issue - KMP in SIAM J. Computing in June, Boyer-Moore in CACM in October). In real I-13 the failure table is a bounded array of small integers (verified fail('ABABAC')=[0,0,1,2,3,0]) and the scan is two advancing indices with character equality; the only awkward part is the list of match positions, the array-return / multiple-return frontier.
spheres.kicker: dart 063 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE HUNGARIAN ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: Harold Kuhn (1955) named it 'Hungarian' to honor Konig & Egervary (1931); Munkres (1957) gave the first polynomial proof (the O(n^3) form came via Tomizawa 1971 / Edmonds-Karp 1972); and Jacobi had it in the 1840s (found only ~2006)
spheres.source: Kuhn 1955; Konig & Egervary 1931; Munkres 1957; Tomizawa 1971 & Edmonds-Karp 1972 (O(n^3)); Jacobi (d.1851, first publ. posthumously in Latin 1865 (Crelle); collected-works reprint 1890, rediscovered by Francois Ollivier ~2006)
spheres.i13_recommend: presses PS-004 (a 2-D array) - the same want Smith-Waterman (054) and knapsack (053) named. The whole method operates on an n-by-n cost matrix (row and column reductions, zero-covering, augmenting paths); I-13's array is 1-D, so an n-by-n matrix is either a flattened row-major 1-D array (index i*n+j, runs today with manual index math) or the genuine 2-D array the box lists. The reductions and coverings are indexed reads and writes; no bignum, no bitwise.
spheres.blurb: Assign n workers to n jobs, each pair with a cost, so the total is smallest - in polynomial time, not by trying all n! matchings. Reduce each row and column by its minimum (subtracting a constant from a whole row or column leaves the optimal assignment unchanged), cover all zeros with the fewest lines, and when n lines are needed a zero-cost perfect assignment exists. The name hides a triple credit story: Harold Kuhn (1955) named it 'the Hungarian method' to HONOUR the earlier Hungarians Denes Konig and Jeno Egervary (1931) whose theorems it rests on - a rare case of an author crediting his sources in the title - while Carl Gustav Jacobi had essentially the algorithm in the 1840s (buried as a subroutine of a differential-equations bound, first published posthumously in Latin in 1865 (Crelle Journal; reprinted in his collected works 1890) and rediscovered only around 2006; Kuhn later wrote 'How Jacobi Beat Me by 100 Years'), and James Munkres gave the first rigorous polynomial proof in 1957 (the crisp O(n^3) form is Tomizawa 1971 and Edmonds-Karp 1972). In real I-13 the cost matrix is a 2-D array (the open want PS-004, with Smith-Waterman-054 and knapsack-053): a flattened row-major 1-D array runs it today (index i*n+j), verified min-cost assignments; a real 2-D array would let the row/column operations read like the textbook.
spheres.kicker: dart 064 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE BURROWS-WHEELER TRANSFORM
spheres.credit: David Wheeler (of EDSAC / the Wheeler jump) devised the transform ~1983, unpublished for a decade; Michael Burrows & Wheeler wrote it up as a 1994 DEC report - the core idea is Wheeler's, 'Burrows-Wheeler' is report order, not invention order
spheres.source: Burrows & Wheeler, DEC SRC Research Report 124, 'A Block-sorting Lossless Data Compression Algorithm', 1994 (transform ~1983); bzip2 by Julian Seward 1996; FM-index by Ferragina & Manzini 2000
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new for the transform itself - rotation indices + a sort + a gather, all bounded-array work over character codes (no bignum, no bitwise). The one aggregate it strains is strings (the campaign's standing aggregate note): the rotations are conceptually substrings, expressed here as start-indices into one array, and the sort compares by those indices. The space-savvy version never materialises the rotations - it sorts suffixes (a suffix array), the same 1-D index-array discipline with a smarter comparator.
spheres.blurb: Take a string, list all its cyclic rotations, sort them, and read off the LAST column - the result looks scrambled, but equal letters now cluster into runs (making it far more compressible), and, astonishingly, the scramble is perfectly reversible (the last column plus stable sorting walks the original back out via the LF-mapping). It is the heart of bzip2 and, as the FM-index, of modern genome aligners that search DNA without decompressing it. The transform itself changes nothing about the data's size - it is a reversible permutation whose whole value is making a downstream compressor dramatically more effective. Credit is a decade in a drawer: David Wheeler - co-inventor of the subroutine and the 'Wheeler jump' on the EDSAC in 1949 - devised the block-sorting transform around 1983 and never published it alone; Michael Burrows recognised its value and wrote it up with Wheeler as a 1994 DEC report, so 'Burrows-Wheeler' is report order, not invention order (the core idea is Wheeler's). In real I-13 the forward transform is rotation start-indices + a sort + a gather, all bounded-array work over character codes (verified BWT('BANANA$')='ANNB$AA', the N's and A's clustering into runs); the one aggregate it leans on is strings - the space-savvy version sorts suffixes, the same 1-D index-array discipline the campaign's sorts already run.
spheres.kicker: dart 065 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: TIMSORT
spheres.credit: Tim Peters designed it for Python in 2002 (shipped Python 2.3, 2003); in 2015 de Gouw, Rot, de Boer, Bubel & Hahnle (KeY prover) found a latent bug - their correctness PROOF failed, exposing it
spheres.source: Peters, CPython Objects/listsort.txt, 2002; de Gouw et al., 'OpenJDK's java.utils.Collection.sort() Is Broken', CAV 2015 (journal version 2017)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - runs, binary insertion, and merge are bounded-array reads/writes with comparisons (no bignum, no bitwise); galloping needs a binary search (dart 042, runs on the array); the merge stack of run boundaries is itself a bounded array. The pointed tie: Timsort's 2015 bug was an ASSUMED-BUT-UNENFORCED invariant (merge_collapse checked only the top 3 runs, not 4) - exactly the failure mode I-13's validator is built to declare rather than trust.
spheres.blurb: The default sort in Python, Java, Android, V8/Node and (until 2024) Rust is not quicksort or mergesort but Timsort: find the runs already in order and merge them, so nearly-sorted data flies through - adaptive, stable, O(n log n) worst case. Tim Peters wrote it for CPython in 2002 (documented in Objects/listsort.txt). Its story is a lesson the corpus takes to heart: for about thirteen years it was ASSUMED correct and deployed at planetary scale, but never formally verified until de Gouw, Rot, de Boer, Bubel and Hahnle tried in 2015 with the KeY theorem prover - and their proof FAILED, exposing a real latent bug (merge_collapse restored its stack invariant by inspecting only the top three pending runs, not four, so on an adversarial input of ~2^26 elements the run stack overflows and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBounds). The flaw originated in Peters's own 2002 code and every port inherited it; the famous headline 'OpenJDK's sort is broken' points at Java, but the defect was Peters's; and OpenJDK's initial fix (Java 8/9) enlarged the run stack rather than the invariant correction the authors preferred, though Java 11 onward adopted the invariant fix as well (also a myth: galloping does not always speed merges - it is adaptively throttled). In real I-13 Timsort is a composition of no-walls the campaign already cleared - run detection, insertion sort, and stable merge over a bounded array (merge two sorted runs -> one), the galloping a binary search (dart 042) - and its bug is the corpus's recurring warning: an instrument that assumes an invariant must enforce it, not trust it.
spheres.kicker: dart 066 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE MERSENNE TWISTER
spheres.credit: Makoto Matsumoto & Takuji Nishimura (Keio University, 1997, publ. 1998) - Nishimura was a master's student of Hikoe Enomoto at Keio and Matsumoto's crucial collaborator, standardly co-credited. The endpoint of the Twisted GFSR program (Matsumoto & Kurita 1992/94)
spheres.source: Matsumoto & Nishimura, 'Mersenne Twister: A 623-dimensionally equidistributed uniform pseudo-random number generator', ACM TOMACS 8(1), 1998
spheres.i13_recommend: the generator core RUNS - the 624-word state is a bounded array, the twist and the output tempering are bitwise xor/shift/and (darts 001/004/029), and the tempering is bit-exact (verified temper(305419896)=729696813). The one wall is the SEEDING: mt[i]=1812433253*(...)+i needs a 32-bit multiply that wraps mod 2^32, which overflows f64's exact range - the same wrap-around-multiply wall the de Bruijn bit-scan (dart 060) surfaced. So I-13 can RUN the Twister from a pre-seeded state today; it just cannot yet COMPUTE the seed expansion exactly.
spheres.blurb: The default random-number generator in Python, R, PHP, Ruby, MATLAB and Excel for two decades: hold a 624-word state, twist it (each word recombined with the next and one 397 ahead, with a shift and a conditional xor), and temper each output with shifts and masks - giving a period of 2^19937 minus 1 (a Mersenne prime, which is why it is named that, and it is engineered not coincidental) and even spread in up to 623 dimensions. Makoto Matsumoto and Takuji Nishimura published it in 1998 (Nishimura, a master's student of Hikoe Enomoto at Keio and Matsumoto's crucial collaborator (standardly co-credited)); it was the endpoint of the Twisted GFSR program Matsumoto ran with Kurita in 1992-94. Its weakness is stark and the authors stated it: MT19937 is a pure F2-linear generator, so observing 624 consecutive outputs lets you invert the tempering (an invertible bijection - 'untempering'), recover the entire state, and predict every future and past output - it is NOT cryptographically secure, and PCG (O'Neill 2014) and xoshiro (Blackman-Vigna) are the smaller, better modern successors. In real I-13 the generator core runs: the 624-word state is a bounded array and the twist and tempering are the integrated bitwise operators (verified temper(305419896)=729696813, bit-exact); the one wall is the seed init multiply (1812433253 times the previous word, mod 2^32), which needs the same wrap-around 32-bit multiply the de Bruijn bit-scan (dart 060) surfaced - so I-13 can run the Twister from a pre-seeded state today, but cannot yet compute the seed expansion exactly.
spheres.kicker: dart 067 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: PAGERANK
spheres.credit: Larry Page & Sergey Brin (Stanford, 1998, project 'BackRub') - but it is a domain-transfer of eigenvector centrality (Pinski & Narin 1976, Bonacich 1972, Katz 1953), with Robin Li's RankDex (developed 1996; US patent filed 1997) and Marchiori's HyperSearch (1997) as link-ranking precedents Page cited
spheres.source: Page & Brin, 'The PageRank Citation Ranking: Bringing Order to the Web', Stanford tech report 1998/99; Pinski & Narin 1976; Kleinberg HITS 1998; Marchiori HyperSearch 1997; Robin Li RankDex patent 1996
spheres.i13_recommend: presses PS-004 (a 2-D array) - the FOURTH dart on it with Smith-Waterman (054), knapsack (053) and the Hungarian algorithm (064). Power iteration is matrix x vector repeated; the link matrix is a genuine 2-D array, and flattened row-major (index i*n+j, like the Hungarian cost matrix) one step runs on the compiler (verified r0=5, r2=3, links as a 1-D row-major array). The multiply-accumulate is array reads and + *; the damping and normalisation are scalar arithmetic; no bignum, no bitwise (ranks are small f64s summing to 1, a natural array fit). The campaign's clearest signal after multiple-return that a matrix type is the next honest addition.
spheres.blurb: The algorithm that launched Google: rank a web page by the chance a random surfer, clicking links forever, lands on it - which is the dominant eigenvector of the link matrix, found by multiplying a vector by the matrix over and over until it stops changing, with a damping factor (~0.85) mixing in a small chance of jumping anywhere so dead-ends don't swallow the score. Larry Page and Sergey Brin built it at Stanford (their 1996 project 'BackRub' grew into it; the PageRank papers are 1998); the name is a double pun on 'web page' and co-inventor Larry Page. It is popularly mythologised as a from-scratch invention but is really a domain-transfer of eigenvector centrality onto the web: Pinski & Narin (1976) already ranked journals as the dominant eigenvector of a column-stochastic citation matrix (the closest precedent), eigenvector centrality is Bonacich (1972) after Katz (1953) and Hubbell (1965), Robin Li's RankDex (developed 1996; US patent filed 1997, granted 1999, later a seed of Baidu) and Massimo Marchiori's HyperSearch (1997, which Page saw presented and cited) already ranked pages by link structure, and Kleinberg's HITS was contemporaneous. What Page and Brin genuinely added was the random-surfer damping/teleportation term that guarantees a unique, well-defined stationary distribution on the messy real web. In real I-13 power iteration is matrix times vector over a link matrix - the open want PS-004 (a 2-D array), the fourth dart on it - and a flattened row-major 1-D array runs one step today (verified r0=5, r2=3), the rank vector a natural f64 array summing to 1.
spheres.kicker: dart 068 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: WAVE FUNCTION COLLAPSE
spheres.credit: Maxim Gumin (mxgmn) released it in 2016 - the name, the minimum-entropy heuristic and the overlapping model are his; the underlying algorithm is Paul Merrell's 'model synthesis' (i3D 2007). Not a plagiarism scandal: Gumin's README credits Merrell
spheres.source: Gumin, WaveFunctionCollapse repo, Sept 2016; Merrell, 'Example-Based Model Synthesis', i3D 2007 / PhD 2009
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the grid is a bounded array, each cell's possibility set is a small bitset (the integrated bitwise & |, darts 001/029), the collapse order uses the seeded PRNG (dart 004), and propagation is neighbour intersection. All landed; WFC is a composition of no-walls. The honest strain is the entropy heuristic (pick the lowest-entropy cell) - a running scalar min over the array, exactly like Dijkstra's (055) extract-min; a heap (dart 062) would speed the choice, but the linear scan runs.
spheres.blurb: Fill a grid so every neighbour is compatible, from a tiny set of rules - the trick behind endless game worlds that always look hand-made. Each cell starts as a superposition of all tiles; repeatedly collapse the most-constrained cell (lowest Shannon entropy) to one legal tile and propagate the consequences to its neighbours until nothing changes, then repeat, restarting on a contradiction. It is constraint propagation - arc-consistency, the AC-3 of Sudoku solvers - wearing a quantum costume: the 'wave function' is a set of possibilities and 'collapse' is a choice. Maxim Gumin (handle mxgmn) released WaveFunctionCollapse in September 2016 and it went viral in game development; his genuine contributions are the evocative name, the minimum-entropy observation heuristic, and the 'overlapping' model that extracts N-by-N patterns from a single bitmap - but the underlying algorithm is Paul Merrell's 'model synthesis', published a full decade earlier (i3D 2007), which already framed generation as constraint satisfaction over example-derived tile adjacencies. Honestly, this is no plagiarism scandal - Gumin's own README acknowledges Merrell, and Merrell's later comparison is measured. It powers town and island generators in games like Bad North and Oskar Stalberg's Townscaper. In real I-13 WFC is a composition of no-walls: the grid is a bounded array, each cell's possibility set a small bitset (the integrated bitwise & |), the collapse order the seeded PRNG (dart 004), propagation a neighbour intersection (verified: a coastline that obeys every rule, 0 contradictions); the one strain is the entropy heuristic, a scalar min over the array like Dijkstra's extract-min that a heap (dart 062) would speed.
spheres.kicker: dart 069 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: MERGE SORT
spheres.credit: John von Neumann wrote it by hand in 1945 for the EDVAC instruction set (a paper program - no machine existed); Goldstine & von Neumann 1948 coded the bottom-up form; Knuth reconstructed and credited it (1970)
spheres.source: von Neumann 1945 (EDVAC); Goldstine & von Neumann, 'Planning and Coding...Part II', 1948; Knuth, 'Von Neumann's First Computer Program', ACM Computing Surveys 2(4), 1970
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the bottom-up form is the natural fit: a width-doubling loop over the array plus a second f64 array as the O(n) buffer, no recursion needed; the merge runs on the compiler (merge [1,3,5,8] and [2,4,7,10] -> out[0]=1, out[5]=7, ties from the left = stable). It is a two-run-in one-run-out pass, a clean motivating case for the paired-array/PS-004 want, and the exact merge Timsort (066) builds on.
spheres.blurb: Split, sort the halves, merge them back - the oldest recursive idea in computing. John von Neumann wrote a meshing (merge) sort by hand in 1945 for the proposed EDVAC instruction set, one of the very first programs anyone wrote (Knuth titled his 1970 reconstruction 'Von Neumann's First Computer Program'); it was a PAPER program, written partly to stress-test whether the new stored-program instruction set could do a non-numerical job (sorting was IBM's punched-card turf, so proving a general computer could sort was pointed), and it was never run because no stored-program machine existed yet. Two honest trims: the merge/meshing of two sorted decks already existed on punched-card collators, so von Neumann's novelty was the full SORT as a stored-program routine; and his actual program was BOTTOM-UP iterative meshing (the form Goldstine & von Neumann coded in 1948), not the recursive top-down divide-and-conquer textbooks draw - that elegant framing is a later retrofit. Merge sort is stable (ties keep input order), always n log n, and needs an O(n) buffer (its trade-off vs quicksort's in-place partition), which made it the archetypal EXTERNAL sort of the tape era and, as natural merge, the heart of Timsort (dart 066). In real I-13 the merge is two read pointers and one write pointer over bounded arrays (verified merge -> out[0]=1, out[5]=7); the bottom-up width-doubling loop needs no recursion, just a second f64 array as the buffer.
spheres.kicker: dart 070 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: SHELLSORT
spheres.credit: Donald L. Shell (1959, General Electric) - the name is his surname, NOT a seashell or a Unix shell; and his own N/2 gap sequence is among the WORST known (Theta(n^2)); the good gaps and the still-open optimum came from later authors
spheres.source: Shell, 'A High-Speed Sorting Procedure', CACM 2(7), 1959; Hibbard, Pratt, Sedgewick; Ciura's empirical sequence 1,4,10,23,57,132,301,701
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - a strict no-wall: it is binary-search-free insertion sort (cousin of dart 042) done at a stride, in place on the array with the gap as the stride; the gap sequence is a small bounded array of integers. No O(n) buffer (unlike merge sort 070), no bad-pivot cliff (unlike quicksort 045). The only mystery is mathematical (the optimal gaps), not one I-13 can or need resolve.
spheres.blurb: Insertion sort is slow because elements crawl one step at a time; Shellsort lets them jump a gap first - sort everything a gap apart (an h-sort), then shrink the gap to 1 - so a small element far from home leaps most of the way early, and the final gap-1 pass runs over a nearly-sorted array. Two durable myths: the NAME honours Donald Shell the person (his own term was 'diminishing increment sort'), nothing to do with seashells or an OS shell; and the inventor gave it BAD gaps - Shell's N/2, N/4, ..., 1 sequence is Theta(n^2) in the worst case (when N is a power of two, even and odd positions never meet until the final pass), so every practical speedup came from later authors (Hibbard's 2^k-1 giving n^1.5, then Pratt, Sedgewick, and Ciura's empirical 1,4,10,23,57,132,301,701). Remarkably for so simple an algorithm, the exact worst-case complexity of the BEST gap sequence is still an unsolved problem. In real I-13 it is a strict no-wall: insertion sort at a stride, in place on the bounded array (no buffer, no bignum, no bitwise), with the gaps a small integer array - the only mystery is the mathematics of the gaps, not the code.
spheres.kicker: dart 071 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE AVL TREE
spheres.credit: Georgy Adelson-Velsky & Evgenii Landis (Soviet mathematicians, 1962) - 'AVL' is TWO people: Adelson-Velsky is one hyphenated surname (A-V) plus Landis (L), often miscounted as three. The FIRST self-balancing binary search tree
spheres.source: Adelson-Velsky & Landis, 'An algorithm for the organization of information', 1962 (Doklady + English translation same year)
spheres.i13_recommend: the aggregate/pointer wall, stated plainly. I-13's array embeds a COMPLETE tree with index arithmetic (the heap, dart 062), but an AVL tree is not complete - it needs genuine node references that rotations relink, which the bounded f64 array cannot express. It can be faked with parallel arrays (key[], left[], right[], height[] as integer indices into a node pool), which runs - the classic pointerless node-arena encoding - but that IS the honest shape of the want. The balance logic (compare heights, rotate) is scalar and runs; only the linked structure is the wall, shared with the trie (074) and red-black tree (073).
spheres.blurb: A binary search tree stays fast only while it stays bushy; feed it already-sorted data and it degenerates into a linked list with O(n) lookups. The AVL tree was the FIRST to keep itself balanced: each node tracks its balance factor (right subtree height minus left), and after every insert the tree walks back up and, at the first node whose balance reaches +/-2, applies a rotation (single or double) to restore +/-1 - keeping the height under about 1.44*log2(n), the tightest of the classic balanced trees, so lookups are fastest at the cost of more rotations on update. Credit is undisputed but the acronym is chronically miscounted: 'AVL' is TWO Soviet mathematicians, Georgy Adelson-Velsky and Evgenii Landis (1962) - 'Adelson-Velsky' is one person's single hyphenated surname, so it is A-V + L, not three people. In real I-13 the AVL tree is the aggregate/pointer wall stated plainly: unlike the heap (dart 062), which embeds a COMPLETE tree in the array with 2i+1/2i+2 index arithmetic, an AVL tree is not complete and needs real node references that rotations relink; the balance logic is scalar and runs, but the linked structure needs a pointerless node-arena (parallel key/left/right/height index arrays) - the honest shape of the want it shares with the trie (074) and red-black tree (073).
spheres.kicker: dart 072 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE RED-BLACK TREE
spheres.credit: Leonidas Guibas & Robert Sedgewick (1978) recoloured Rudolf Bayer's 1972 'symmetric binary B-tree' (a binary encoding of the 2-3-4 tree); the two-colour framing made it teachable. The balanced tree in std::map, Java TreeMap, the Linux scheduler
spheres.source: Guibas & Sedgewick, 'A Dichromatic Framework for Balanced Trees', FOCS 1978; Bayer, symmetric binary B-trees, 1972; the node-colour vs link-colour reformulation is CLRS
spheres.i13_recommend: the SAME aggregate/pointer wall as AVL (072) and the trie (074) - heap-allocated nodes with references the rebalancing relinks. The colour is one bit (the integrated bitwise handles it trivially), the rules (compare black-heights, check red-red) are scalar and run; only the node graph is the want. The pointerless node-arena encoding (key/left/right/colour as parallel arrays into a pool) runs on I-13's arrays. Three darts now land on the same frontier - AVL, red-black, and the trie all want heap-allocated linked nodes.
spheres.blurb: The balanced search tree that actually runs your code: C++ std::map/std::set, Java TreeMap/TreeSet, the Linux CFS scheduler and kernel timers. It colours each node red or black and keeps two rules - no red node has a red child, and every root-to-leaf path has the same number of black nodes - which alone forces the height within 2*log2(n) of perfect; an insert that breaks the rules is fixed by recolouring plus at most a couple of rotations, far fewer than AVL needs (looser balance, cheaper updates - why libraries pick it for general maps and AVL for lookup-heavy work). The popular 'Guibas and Sedgewick invented it in 1978' overstates it: the data structure IS Rudolf Bayer's 1972 symmetric binary B-tree (a binary encoding of the 2-3-4 tree); Guibas and Sedgewick's contribution was the two-colour abstraction and a uniform rebalancing framework that made it teachable. And originally the colour marked the LINK to a node ('this child is part of the same B-tree node'); the familiar 'the node is red' is the later CLRS reformulation. In real I-13 it is the same aggregate/pointer wall as AVL (072) and the trie (074): the colour is one bit (trivial bitwise), the rules are scalar and run, but the linked node graph needs a pointerless node-arena - three darts now on one frontier, heap-allocated linked nodes.
spheres.kicker: dart 073 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE TRIE
spheres.credit: Edward Fredkin NAMED it ('Trie Memory', 1960, from reTRIEval) - but Rene de la Briandais had the linked-children structure a year earlier (1959), and Axel Thue the abstract idea in 1912. Fredkin intended it pronounced 'tree'; 'try' is the retrofit
spheres.source: Fredkin, 'Trie Memory', CACM 3(9), 1960; de la Briandais 1959; Thue 1912; Morrison's PATRICIA/radix tree 1968
spheres.i13_recommend: the aggregate wall, doubled - strings (the keys are character sequences) AND dynamically linked nodes (a child per letter). It joins AVL (072) and red-black (073) on the linked-node want, plus the campaign's standing string want (Boyer-Moore-061, KMP-063, BWT-065). A trie flattens into a node arena (a 2-D children table as parallel index arrays), which runs on I-13's arrays for a fixed alphabet - the same pointerless encoding the other trees need, over a bounded alphabet. A cluster of darts (three trees + the string algorithms) now want heap-allocated linked structure over sequences, the corpus's largest un-added aggregate.
spheres.blurb: Store a set of words so shared beginnings are stored once: a tree where each edge is a letter and each root-to-node path spells a prefix, so every word sharing a prefix shares nodes up to where they diverge - and autocomplete, spell-check, and longest-prefix IP routing become a single walk down the tree. Two myths: Edward Fredkin is called the inventor but he NAMED it (coining 'trie' from reTRIEval in his 1960 CACM paper 'Trie Memory'), while Rene de la Briandais had published the linked-list-of-children structure a year earlier (1959) and Axel Thue described the string-set idea abstractly in 1912; and the pronunciation runs opposite to what most assume - Fredkin intended 'trie' to sound like 'tree' (from reTRIEval), and 'try' is the later retrofit adopted to avoid the collision with 'tree'. Donald Morrison's 1968 PATRICIA/radix tree compresses single-child chains into the space-efficient trie that routers and suffix structures use. In real I-13 the trie stacks two standing wants - strings (character-sequence keys) and dynamically linked nodes (a child per letter) - joining AVL (072) and red-black (073) on the linked-node frontier and the string algorithms (Boyer-Moore-061, KMP-063, BWT-065); it flattens into a node arena (a children table as parallel index arrays over a fixed alphabet), which runs on the bounded array.
spheres.kicker: dart 074 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE CYCLIC REDUNDANCY CHECK
spheres.credit: W. Wesley Peterson & D. T. Brown (1961) gave the general theory of cyclic codes - but the ubiquitous CRC-32 polynomial (0x04C11DB7) is LATER (AUTODIN-II ~1975, cemented by Ethernet). A CRC is a LINEAR function, NOT a cryptographic hash
spheres.source: Peterson & Brown, 'Cyclic Codes for Error Detection', Proc. IRE, 1961; CRC-32 poly from AUTODIN-II (Hammond-Brown-Liu RADC-TR-75-138, 1975) & IEEE 802.3
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - a strict no-wall: the whole computation is & << ^ over integers that stay within f64's exact range (a byte-at-a-time CRC keeps values under 2^32); the 256-entry table variant is a bounded array, the bit-at-a-time variant pure bitwise. Verified bit-exact: CRC-8 (poly 0x07) of 0x42 = 201 (0xC9), and appending it then re-checking gives 0 (a flipped bit gives nonzero, caught). Conceptually it is the EXTERNAL checksum the corpus mostly avoids - rev-e's point is that a palindrome needs none; the CRC is the honest counter-example, the check you bolt on when data is not self-mirroring.
spheres.blurb: Every Ethernet frame, ZIP file, and PNG carries a CRC: read the data bits as the coefficients of a polynomial over GF(2) (arithmetic where 1+1=0, i.e. XOR), divide by a fixed generator polynomial, and append the remainder as the check; the receiver re-divides and expects zero, so a clean message passes and a corrupted one does not. Two misattributions: W. Wesley Peterson & D. T. Brown (1961) gave the general THEORY of cyclic codes and the shift-register hardware, but the ubiquitous CRC-32 generator (0x04C11DB7) that everyone actually runs comes from mid-1970s AUTODIN-II work and Ethernet, not from Peterson; and a CRC is routinely mis-called a hash - it is a LINEAR function, so an adversary can edit the message and fix the CRC to match, meaning it guards against noise, not malice. A good degree-n polynomial catches all burst errors shorter than n bits, all single/double-bit errors, and all odd numbers of flips - exactly what a wire produces. In real I-13 it is a strict no-wall: the whole computation is shift, test the top bit, conditional XOR with the polynomial, over integers under 2^32 (verified CRC-8 of 0x42 = 201 = 0xC9, re-check 0, one flipped bit caught). And it is the honest counter-example to the corpus's own seal: rev-e's principle is that a palindrome is its OWN checksum (needs none); the CRC is the external remainder you bolt on when the data does not read the same both ways.
spheres.kicker: dart 075 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE EUCLIDEAN RHYTHM
spheres.credit: E. Bjorklund (2003) wrote the algorithm - for a particle-accelerator/neutron-source timing gate; Godfried Toussaint recognised it (2004) IS Euclid's GCD (~300 BCE) and that its outputs are the world's traditional rhythms, naming it in his 2005 survey; Toussaint credits Bjorklund plainly
spheres.source: Toussaint, 'The Euclidean Algorithm Generates Traditional Musical Rhythms', 2004; Bjorklund 2003 (Spallation Neutron Source timing); Euclid, Elements, c.300 BCE
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the placement is the Euclidean FOLD the campaign already runs (Euclid's GCD, dart 027, and std/gcd.i13), writing into a bounded array of n beats; integer subtraction/remainder and array writes, no bignum, no bitwise. A lovely closure: dart 027 built Euclid's GCD as pure arithmetic, and this dart shows the very same fold, pointed at n beats instead of two integers, is the hidden grammar of human rhythm - one algorithm, two millennia apart, both running in the counted language.
spheres.blurb: Spread k beats as evenly as possible over n pulses and you get, note for note, the traditional rhythms of Cuba, Turkey, West Africa and beyond - the Cuban tresillo E(3,8) = x..x..x. (verified), the cinquillo E(5,8), Turkish aksak E(4,9), sub-Saharan bell patterns. The startling part is that the algorithm which spaces them is EUCLID's: E. Bjorklund wrote it in 2003 to fire a timing gate k times as evenly as possible over n intervals for a spallation neutron source (a particle accelerator, no music in sight), and Godfried Toussaint recognised (2004) that Bjorklund's algorithm has the same structure as Euclid's ~300 BCE greatest-common-divisor algorithm - repeated pairing/subtraction, the leftover after each round becoming the next round's divisor - surveyed its outputs against real world music, and gave it the name in his 2005 survey 'The Euclidean Algorithm Generates Traditional Musical Rhythms' (crediting Bjorklund plainly). 'Most even' is what makes a groove feel right, and 'most even' is a number-theory fact, not a musical one. In real I-13 there is nothing new: the placement is the Euclidean fold the campaign already runs (Euclid's GCD, dart 027, and std/gcd.i13), writing into a bounded array of n beats - the very same fold that dart 027 built for two integers, pointed instead at n beats, and it is the hidden grammar of human rhythm, both running in the counted language.
spheres.kicker: dart 076 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: XIAOLIN WU'S LINE
spheres.credit: Xiaolin Wu (1991, U. of Western Ontario) - for the EFFICIENT incremental form; he did not invent antialiased lines (Gupta & Sproull had them in 1981 via a filtered-distance table). The paper is titled 'An Efficient Antialiasing Technique' and covers circles too
spheres.source: Wu, 'An Efficient Antialiasing Technique', SIGGRAPH Computer Graphics 25(4), 1991; Gupta & Sproull 1981; Bresenham 1962/65 (dart 003)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - nothing new - the pixel intensity is 1 - frac(y) and its complement (the two straddling pixels' coverages sum to 1), advanced by the slope each step. Add, floor, fraction - all f64 the compiler has; the output grid is the array, the intensities are f64. (Wu's own 1991 method is integer/fixed-point - his abstract boasts even less integer arithmetic than Bresenham; the f64 coverage form here is the later popularized pseudocode, the corpus's reimplementation choice.) A neat pair with dart 003: same slope, same walk; Bresenham rounds coverage to 0/1 (jagged), Wu keeps the fraction (smooth), both integer at heart - the campaign has now run both faces of the oldest graphics primitive.
spheres.blurb: Bresenham's line (dart 003) is fast but jagged - each pixel is fully on or off, so a shallow diagonal stair-steps. Xiaolin Wu's line keeps Bresenham's speed but colours two pixels per step, their brightness set by how much of each the ideal line covers (the coverages sum to 1), and the eye blends the stairs into a smooth stroke. Two honest caveats: 'Xiaolin Wu's line algorithm' is a later community eponym - the 1991 paper is titled 'An Efficient Antialiasing Technique' and covers circles too; and Wu did NOT invent antialiased line drawing - Gupta & Sproull (1981) drew the straddling pixels with intensities from a precomputed filtered-distance table a decade earlier. Wu's genuine contribution is EFFICIENCY: he re-derives the coverage as a simple incremental computation (an error accumulator like Bresenham's) plus a symmetry trick drawing from both ends, so antialiasing costs almost nothing extra. In real I-13 it is nothing new: Wu's own 1991 method is integer/fixed-point too (his abstract boasts even LESS integer arithmetic than Bresenham); the f64 form here - the intensity is 1 minus the fractional part of y and its complement, advanced by the slope each step (add, floor, fraction, all f64) - is the popularized pseudocode and the I-13 reimplementation's choice. A neat pair with dart 003, the same slope and walk, one rounding coverage to 0/1 (jagged), the other keeping the fraction (smooth); both integer at heart.
spheres.kicker: dart 077 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE K-D TREE
spheres.credit: Jon Louis Bentley coined the k-d tree in 1975 (as a Stanford undergraduate) - but the 1975 paper already gave a nearest-neighbour search (empirically O(log n)), but the OPTIMIZED tree and the rigorous PROOF of expected-logarithmic NN time that everyone cites are Friedman, Bentley & Finkel 1977. The point quadtree (Finkel & Bentley 1974) is the direct ancestor; 'a k-d tree is a special case of a BSP tree' is retroactive (BSP came in 1980, five years later); the 'k' is a variable, not an acronym
spheres.source: Bentley, 'Multidimensional binary search trees used for associative searching', CACM 18(9), 1975; Friedman, Bentley & Finkel, 'An algorithm for finding best matches in logarithmic expected time', ACM TOMS 3(3), 1977; Finkel & Bentley, point quadtree, Acta Informatica 4(1), 1974
spheres.i13_recommend: BUILD (recursion + median split + f64 comparisons) and SEARCH (recursive descent, backtrack, squared distance dx*dx+dy*dy compared against the best - no sqrt, stays f64) run on the compiler; verified query q=(8,5) among six points: the first leaf (8,1) is at distance^2 16 and is NOT the answer, backtracking finds the true nearest (9,6) at distance^2 2. The wall is genuine node references (each internal node points to a left and right child) - PS-015, shared with AVL (072), red-black (073), the trie (074) - faked with a node arena (left[], right[], axis[] plus coordinate arrays), the move that closed heap-on-array (PS-005/062). A second want: the points are pairs (x,y), and i13 arrays hold f64 only, so the point set is parallel x[]/y[] arrays (PS-014 kin), not an array of tuples.
spheres.blurb: Split a cloud of points with axis-aligned planes on alternating axes (x, then y, then x, ...) and nearest-neighbour search stops being a scan of every point and becomes a walk down a tree that PRUNES whole regions: descend to the leaf whose region holds the query, keep it as the current best, then climb back up and only dip into a sibling subtree if the query's distance to the splitting plane is less than the current best radius. The catch that makes it correct is the backtrack - the first leaf you land in is usually NOT the true nearest (verified: query (8,5) first reaches leaf (8,1) at distance 4, but the true nearest is (9,6) at distance sqrt(2), found only on the way back up). Credit is routinely misdated: Jon Bentley coined the k-d tree in 1975 (his Stanford undergraduate work, BS 1974, though the paper itself came from UNC), and that 1975 paper already gave a nearest-neighbour search with an empirically-observed O(log n) alongside region/partial/exact-match queries; what Friedman, Bentley & Finkel 1977 added was the OPTIMIZED tree (max-spread split, points in leaf buckets) and the rigorous PROOF of expected-logarithmic NN time via the bounds-overlap-ball test - the version people actually cite. The point quadtree (Finkel & Bentley 1974) is the direct ancestor; 'a k-d tree is a special case of a BSP tree' is backwards, since BSP trees came in 1980; and 'k' is a variable (2-d tree, 3-d tree), not an acronym. In real I-13 the whole numeric spine runs (build, backtracking search, squared-distance in f64 - verified first-leaf 16 corrected to nearest 2); the wall is the linked left/right node references (PS-015, shared with AVL-072, red-black-073, trie-074), expressible as a pointerless node arena, and a quieter want is that the points are (x,y) pairs held as parallel f64 arrays.
spheres.kicker: dart 078 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: TARJAN'S SCC ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: Robert Tarjan (1972) - the single-pass lowlink is genuinely his, but DFS itself is 19th-century (Tremaux's maze rule), and SCC-via-DFS predates him (Purdom 1970, Munro 1971). The Tarjan-vs-Kosaraju chronology is usually told BACKWARDS: Tarjan published in 1972, Kosaraju's two-pass method was unpublished/later. 'Tarjan's algorithm' is ambiguous - he also owns biconnected components, offline LCA, Fibonacci heaps, link-cut trees
spheres.source: Tarjan, 'Depth-first search and linear graph algorithms', SIAM J. Comput. 1(2), 1972; Purdom 1970; Munro 1971; DFS attributed to Charles Tremaux (19th c.)
spheres.i13_recommend: recursion is I-13's home turf and the graph rides on bounded arrays (index[], lowlink[], onStack[], an explicit stack); verified the whole vertex set reached over an edge list (5 nodes, edges 0-1-2-0 and 2-3, 3-4-3 -> total 5 reachable from node 0, SCCs {0,1,2} and {3,4}). The friction is Tarjan's IN-PLACE shared stack and lowlink minimisation - value semantics (no aliasing) turns it into threading one state array through every return (the node-arena pattern); it runs that way, but a genuine tuple return would make it natural - a fresh, sharp nudge toward multiple-return, the sole withheld frontier (045/048/052/055/059).
spheres.blurb: A strongly connected component is a maximal set of nodes that can all reach each other; Tarjan finds every one in a SINGLE depth-first traversal - no second pass - by tracking for each node the oldest node still on the stack that its subtree can climb back to (the lowlink). When a node finishes with lowlink equal to its own index, it is the root of an SCC and the stack is popped down to it. Three credit corrections: Tarjan did NOT invent depth-first search (it is a 19th-century maze-walking rule attributed to Tremaux; Tarjan with Hopcroft turned it into a linear-time tool); the chronology against Kosaraju is usually reversed (people assume the two-pass 'Kosaraju' method is the original and Tarjan the later trick, but Tarjan published in 1972 and Kosaraju's method was unpublished/later); and Tarjan was not the first to find strong components with DFS (Purdom 1970 and Munro 1971 both did, before 1972) - his genuine first is the single-pass lowlink. The lowlink is also routinely mis-stated: it is the smallest index of a node STILL ON THE STACK reachable through the subtree plus at most one back/cross edge. In real I-13 the DFS recursion and the index/lowlink/onStack arrays are exactly what runs (verified: all 5 nodes reached over an edge list, giving SCCs {1,2,3} and {4,5}); the friction is Tarjan's in-place shared stack and lowlink updates, which value semantics turns into threading one state array through returns - a sharp fresh nudge toward multiple-return.
spheres.kicker: dart 079 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: THE VITERBI ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: Andrew Viterbi (1967) - who called his own method 'clearly suboptimal' and impractical, using it only to prove an error bound (already derived by Howard Yudkin, MIT thesis 1964). G. David Forney coined the word 'trellis' and recognised the optimum trellis decoder in a 1967 report (before Omura), then proved maximum-likelihood optimality and fixed the name in his 1973 tutorial; Jim Omura showed (1968/69) it is just Bellman's forward dynamic programming. Viterbi never named it after himself
spheres.source: Viterbi, 'Error bounds for convolutional codes and an asymptotically optimum decoding algorithm', IEEE Trans. Info. Theory, 1967; Forney, 'The Viterbi Algorithm', Proc. IEEE 61(3), 1973; Omura 1969; Yudkin (MIT thesis) 1964
spheres.i13_recommend: the DP itself has no wall - verified the health-HMM decode (obs [normal, cold, dizzy] -> best probability 0.01512, most-likely path Healthy, Healthy, Fever). The natural home is a 2-D array (states x time) = PS-004, the want named by knapsack (053), Smith-Waterman (054), Hungarian (064), PageRank (068) - but it runs today flattened into a 1-D array with index arithmetic t*S+s, exactly as those darts do; the back-pointer table is a parallel integer array, and path recovery is a backward walk through it.
spheres.blurb: Given noisy observations and a model of hidden states, which single path of states most likely produced them? Viterbi answers with dynamic programming on a trellis: for each state at each time keep the best score of any path ending there, plus a back-pointer; at the end take the best final state and follow the pointers back. It decodes convolutional codes, GSM/CDMA, speech, and DNA. The story is thick with irony: Andrew Viterbi (1967) called his own method 'clearly suboptimal' and impractical, introducing it only to prove an error bound - and even that bound had already been derived by Howard Yudkin (MIT, 1964). It is just forward dynamic programming (Bellman's 1950s method) applied to a trellis, as Jim Omura showed in 1968-69. The name and the very word 'trellis' - the diagram every textbook teaches it with - are G. David Forney's, who recognised it as an optimum trellis decoder and coined 'trellis' in a 1967 NASA Ames report (the same year as Viterbi, before Omura), then PROVED it maximum-likelihood optimal and fixed the name in his canonical 1973 Proc. IEEE tutorial 'The Viterbi Algorithm'; Viterbi never named it after himself. In real I-13 the DP has no wall (verified best 0.01512, path Healthy-Healthy-Fever); its natural home is a 2-D states-by-time array (PS-004, with knapsack-053, Smith-Waterman-054, Hungarian-064, PageRank-068) but it runs today flattened into a 1-D array with t*S+s indexing, the back-pointer table a parallel integer array.
spheres.kicker: dart 080 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: STRASSEN'S ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: Volker Strassen (1968 discovery, 1969 paper 'Gaussian elimination is not optimal', Numer. Math. 13:354-356) - who was trying to prove the OPPOSITE, that 8 multiplications are necessary. Shmuel Winograd (1971) proved 6 impossible, so 7 is optimal - the lower bound is Winograd's, not Strassen's. The popular 7-mult/15-addition form is WINOGRAD's variant (Strassen's original used 18 additions) = Strassen-Winograd; 'inspired by Karatsuba' is an undocumented modern teaching retrofit
spheres.source: Strassen, 'Gaussian elimination is not optimal', Numerische Mathematik 13, 354-356, 1969; Winograd 1971 (optimality of 7 multiplications for 2x2); cf. Karatsuba 1962 (dart 041)
spheres.i13_recommend: the seven products and the recombination are scalar add/subtract/multiply - verified [[1,2],[3,4]] x [[5,6],[7,8]] -> M1=65 .. M7=-30 -> C=[[19,22],[43,50]], identical to the 8-multiplication schoolbook product using only 7 multiplications. The natural container is a 2-D array (a matrix) = PS-004 again; today the four entries live in a flat length-4 array, and recursion on blocks would use index arithmetic. It is the matrix analogue of Karatsuba (dart 041): both buy a cheaper multiply with extra additions. A genuine 2-D array would let the recursive block form read verbatim - the strongest single case yet for PS-004.
spheres.blurb: Multiplying two 2x2 matrices seems to need eight scalar multiplications; Strassen found a way with SEVEN, and because it applies recursively to blocks, matrix multiplication drops from n^3 to about n^2.807 - the shock that opened the whole field of fast matrix multiplication (whose optimal exponent is still an open problem creeping toward 2). The popular story gets three things wrong: Strassen (1968-69) was trying to prove the OPPOSITE - that 8 multiplications are necessary - and found 7 instead; he did NOT prove 7 optimal (Shmuel Winograd proved 6 impossible in 1971, so the lower bound is Winograd's); and the fast version everyone codes (7 multiplications, 15 additions) is WINOGRAD's variant, not Strassen's original (which used 18 additions) - fairly it is Strassen-Winograd. The common 'Strassen was directly inspired by Karatsuba (dart 041)' is a modern pedagogical retrofit; the 1969 paper cites no such influence, though the kinship (buy a cheaper multiply with extra additions) is real. In real I-13 the seven products and the recombination are pure scalar arithmetic - verified [[1,2],[3,4]] x [[5,6],[7,8]] gives C=[[19,22],[43,50]] with 7 multiplications (M1=65 through M7=-30), identical to the schoolbook product; the container is a 2-D array (a matrix), PS-004, today a flat length-4 array, recursion on blocks using index arithmetic - the matrix analogue of Karatsuba.
