spheres.title: VERLET INTEGRATION
spheres.credit: 'Verlet integration' is a naming accident (Stigler's law): Loup Verlet (1967, molecular dynamics) popularized it but the method is ~176 years older. The earliest documented use is Delambre (1791, astronomy); Newton's Principia (1687, Book 1 Prop. 1) is provably a second-order symplectic/leapfrog integrator; Carl Stormer used it (1907, auroral particle paths) so it is also 'Stormer's method' / 'Stormer-Verlet', and astronomers call the same scheme 'Cowell's method'. 'Velocity Verlet' is Swope, Andersen, Berens & Wilson (1982), not Verlet's
spheres.source: Verlet, 'Computer Experiments on Classical Fluids', Phys. Rev. 159, 1967; Stormer 1907; Newton, Principia, Book 1 Prop. 1, 1687; Swope, Andersen, Berens & Wilson 1982 (Velocity Verlet)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - a strict no-wall like Newton-Raphson (026), CORDIC (009), Box-Muller (033): next = 2*cur - prev + a*dt*dt, all f64 the compiler already has. Verified for constant acceleration x(t)=5*t^2 with dt=0.1: the recurrence lands exactly on x2=0.2, x3=0.45, x4=0.8, x5=1.25 (Verlet is EXACT for constant acceleration). A trajectory over many steps is a bounded array of positions. Its virtue - energy conservation / symplecticity - is exactly the structural honesty the corpus prizes: not faster, but stable over long horizons where Euler quietly drifts.
spheres.blurb: To move a simulated particle forward, the obvious Euler step (position += velocity*dt) slowly leaks energy and orbits spiral apart; Verlet integration - next = 2*current - previous + acceleration*dt^2, with velocity never appearing - is time-reversible and symplectic, so orbits stay closed for millions of steps. It runs cloth, ragdolls, molecular dynamics, and half the physics engines shipping today. The name is a textbook accident (Stigler's law): Loup Verlet (1967) only popularized it for molecular dynamics; the scheme is ~176 years older. Its earliest documented use is Delambre in 1791 (astronomy); Newton's Principia (1687, Book 1 Proposition 1) - the coast-then-kick polygon proving Kepler's area law - is provably a second-order symplectic (leapfrog) integrator; Carl Stormer used it in 1907 for auroral charged-particle trajectories, so numerical analysts call it 'Stormer's method' or 'Stormer-Verlet' and astronomers call the identical scheme 'Cowell's method'. 'Velocity Verlet' is later still (Swope, Andersen, Berens & Wilson, 1982) and produces the identical position path. In real I-13 it is a strict no-wall: the whole step is f64 add and multiply over the last two scalars, and it reproduces the exact analytic parabola of constant-acceleration motion - verified x(t)=5t^2 at dt=0.1 landing on 0.2, 0.45, 0.8, 1.25 to the digit; a trajectory is a bounded array of positions, and the virtue is structural (energy conservation over long horizons where Euler drifts).

spheres.title: POLLARD'S P-1 METHOD
spheres.credit: John Pollard (1974) - a year before his more famous rho method (1975); the two are constantly confused (smoothness vs cycle-finding, different papers, different years, same author). The 'exploit p-1's factorization' insight predates Pollard (standard in primality testing - Pocklington, Lucas); the two-stage/large-prime continuation is already in Pollard's ORIGINAL 1974 paper (Montgomery 1987 only sped it up). Lenstra's ECM (1985) is literally p-1 generalized; Williams' p+1 (1982) is the sibling
spheres.source: Pollard, 'Theorems on factorization and primality testing', Proc. Cambridge Phil. Soc. 76, 1974; Pollard rho 1975 (BIT 15); Lenstra, elliptic-curve method, 1985; Williams p+1, 1982
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - self-referential: modular exponentiation (darts 032, 035, 050) and Euclid's gcd (027, std/gcd.i13) both landed already, and together they split n on the real compiler. Verified n=1927, base 2, exponent 120: a = 2^120 mod 1927 = 1395, gcd(1394, 1927) = 41, so 1927 = 41 x 47 (41-1 = 40 is 5-smooth and divides 120, so 41 emerges; 47-1 = 46 is not smooth for this bound, so it does not); a too-small bound finds nothing. With bignum the same code scales past f64's ceiling. A third dart whose payoff is prior additions COMPOUNDING - two landed features, no new primitive, a real factorization out the other end.
spheres.blurb: To split a composite n, Pollard's p-1 method gambles that some prime factor p has a p-1 built only from small primes (p-1 is 'smooth'). Then for a smooth exponent M = lcm(1..B), a = 2^M mod n satisfies a = 1 mod p by Fermat's little theorem, so p divides a-1 and gcd(a-1, n) hands you p - Fermat's little theorem turned into a crowbar. Credit is honest (Pollard really invented it in 1974) but hedged three ways: it is a YEAR BEFORE his more famous rho method (1975), and the two are perpetually confused despite being different ideas (smoothness vs Floyd cycle-finding, dart 040); the 'exploit p-1's factorization' insight is older than Pollard (standard in primality testing, Pocklington and Lucas); and the two-stage large-prime continuation is already in Pollard's original 1974 paper, not a later Montgomery add-on (Montgomery 1987 only sped it up). Lenstra's elliptic-curve method (1985) is literally p-1 generalized (swap the group (Z/pZ)* of order p-1 for an elliptic curve whose order you can re-roll), and Williams' p+1 (1982) is the sibling. In real I-13 it factors on the compiler using only prior additions - modexp (032/035/050) and Euclid's gcd (027) - verified n=1927 -> 2^120 mod 1927 = 1395, gcd(1394,1927) = 41, giving 1927 = 41 x 47; with bignum it scales past f64.

spheres.title: THE EXTENDED EUCLIDEAN ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: The coefficient algorithm is Aryabhata's kuttaka ('pulverizer', c. 499 CE, Aryabhatiya Ganitapada 32-33) - roughly 1,130 years before Bachet and 1,280 before Bezout; Bhaskara I (c. 629 CE) named it kuttaka and wrote the exposition (Aryabhata stated it tersely, unnamed). 'Bezout's identity' for INTEGERS is a naming accident - Etienne Bezout (1779) proved the POLYNOMIAL version, the integer statement was Bachet's (1624), the name stuck via Bourbaki (~1949); Granville's 2024 note is titled 'It is not Bezout's identity'
spheres.source: Aryabhata, Aryabhatiya (Ganitapada 32-33), c.499 CE; Bhaskara I, c.629 CE (naming 'kuttaka'); Bachet, 1624 (integer case); Bezout, Theorie generale des equations algebriques, 1779 (polynomial case); A. Granville, 'It is not Bezout's identity', 2024
spheres.i13_recommend: the clearest MULTIPLE-RETURN case in the whole campaign: the natural signature is (g, s, t) = extgcd(a, b), three values at once, the sole withheld frontier (named by quicksort-045, union-find-048, A*-052, Dijkstra-055, FFT-059). The gcd part runs, and threaded down to a single value it lands the inverse - verified inverse of 7 mod 26: the Bezout coefficient s = -11 gives 7^-1 = 15 (mod 26), check 7*15 mod 26 = 1. And because 26 is COMPOSITE, Fermat's a^(p-2) trick is unavailable, so extended Euclid is the only road, which makes the triple return feel less like a convenience and more like the honest shape. Until a tuple lands, the corpus returns s alone and reconstructs.
spheres.blurb: Euclid's algorithm (dart 027) gives the gcd of a and b; the extended version also returns two integers s, t with s*a + t*b = gcd - and when the gcd is 1, that s is the modular inverse of a, the workhorse behind RSA, the Chinese remainder theorem, and every 'divide mod n'. Run the remainder ladder but carry a pair of coefficients alongside each remainder; when the remainder hits 0 the previous row holds gcd = s*a + t*b. The credit runs deep and misattributed: the algorithm that produces the coefficients is Aryabhata's kuttaka ('pulverizer', c. 499 CE), about 1,130 years before Bachet and 1,280 before Bezout, with Bhaskara I (c. 629 CE) naming and expounding it; and 'Bezout's identity' for INTEGERS is itself a naming accident - Etienne Bezout (1779) proved the POLYNOMIAL version, the integer statement was Bachet's (1624), and the name stuck only through Bourbaki (~1949), as Andrew Granville's 2024 note 'It is not Bezout's identity' documents. Euclid gave the gcd loop but not the explicit symbolic coefficients. In real I-13 this is the sharpest multiple-return case yet: the natural signature (g, s, t) hands back three values at once (the sole withheld frontier, with quicksort-045, union-find-048, A*-052, Dijkstra-055, FFT-059); threaded to a single value it still runs (verified 7^-1 = 15 mod 26 via s = -11, check 7*15 mod 26 = 1), and because 26 is composite Fermat's inverse trick is unavailable, so extended Euclid is the only road - the triple return is the honest shape.

spheres.title: THE GRAY-SCOTT MODEL
spheres.credit: Alan Turing (1952, 'The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis' - his last paper in biology - he published on the Riemann zeta in 1953 and computability in 1954 before his death in 1954) predicted diffusion-driven instability - his genuine novelty: diffusion, normally smoothing, can CREATE pattern. He was not first to a reaction-diffusion PDE (KPP 1937, Rashevsky 1940). The famous 'Gray-Scott patterns' are NOT Gray & Scott's: they (1983-85) studied only a WELL-MIXED reactor with no space, and their kinetics are a variant of Sel'kov's 1968 glycolysis model; John Pearson (1993) ran Gray-Scott ON A GRID and produced the iconic patterns; the first real chemical Turing pattern was Castets/Dulos/Boissonade/De Kepper (1990)
spheres.source: Turing, 'The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis', Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 237, 1952; Pearson, 'Complex Patterns in a Simple System', Science 261, 1993; Gray & Scott 1983-85; Sel'kov 1968; Castets, Dulos, Boissonade & De Kepper 1990
spheres.i13_recommend: the field is a 2-D grid = PS-004 once more, and every cell's update is f64 arithmetic - the autocatalytic reaction term R = u*v*v grounds at 0.03125 on the compiler, and the whole tick is add/multiply (like Life-020 or the Mandelbrot escape-019). It runs today flattened into a 1-D array with y*W+x indexing plus a second buffer for the next tick. Emergence for free - no wall, just a grid and a rule; the pattern is not stored anywhere, it is COMPUTED into being, which is the corpus's whole thesis in a dish.
spheres.blurb: Two chemicals sit on a grid: one diffuses fast, one slow, and they react (v eats u autocatalytically as u*v^2, u is fed at rate F, v removed at rate F+k). From an almost-uniform start, spots, stripes, and coral self-organize - no designer, just local rules, and tiny changes in F and k flip the whole grid between mitosis-like spots, worms, and waves. Alan Turing predicted this 'diffusion-driven instability' in 1952, in 'The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis' - his last paper IN BIOLOGY (he published on the Riemann zeta in 1953 and computability in 1954 before his death), often mis-placed near his 1936-1950 computing work - and his genuine novelty was the counter-intuitive result that diffusion, which normally smooths, can CREATE pattern (he was not first to a reaction-diffusion PDE; KPP 1937 and Rashevsky's 1940 cell-polarity diffusion came earlier). The famous 'Gray-Scott patterns' (spots that split, worms, coral) are NOT Gray & Scott's: they (1983-85) only ever studied a WELL-MIXED reactor with no spatial dimension, and their kinetics are a variant of Sel'kov's 1968 glycolysis model; John Pearson (1993) ran Gray-Scott on a GRID and produced the now-iconic zoo, and the first real chemical Turing pattern was made by Castets, Dulos, Boissonade & De Kepper in 1990 - a 38-year gap between prediction and dish. In real I-13 the field is a 2-D grid (PS-004) and every cell's update is f64 arithmetic - the reaction term R = u*v^2 grounds at 0.03125, the whole tick add and multiply (like Life-020, Mandelbrot-019) - running flattened into a 1-D array with y*W+x indexing; the pattern is not stored, it is computed into being.

spheres.title: THE BEZIER CURVE
spheres.credit: Paul de Casteljau (Citroen, 1959) invented the repeated-lerp algorithm but Citroen kept it a trade secret and forbade publication; Pierre Bezier (Renault, early 1960s) reached the same curves independently using control VECTORS and was allowed to patent/publish (UNISURF 1968), so the CURVE carries his name while the ALGORITHM carries de Casteljau's - two different men. The underlying math is Sergei Bernstein's basis (1912); Forrest 1972 spotted the connection; de Casteljau published his own account only in 1985
spheres.source: de Casteljau (Citroen internal 'poles', 1959; 'Formes a poles', Hermes 1985); Bezier UNISURF 1968; Bernstein 1912; A. R. Forrest, Computer Journal 15(1), 1972
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - a strict no-wall in the family of Bresenham (003) and Verlet (082): the whole algorithm is lerp(a,b,t)=a+(b-a)*t, pure f64 (one subtract, one multiply, one add per coordinate). The control points are (x,y) PAIRS - the PS-014 pair want - but the wall is SIDESTEPPED, not hit: hold them as two parallel f64 arrays x[]=[0,1,3,4], y[]=[0,3,3,0] and let the triangular cascade overwrite them in place (verified cubic at t=0.5 -> (2.0, 2.25), matching the Bernstein closed form exactly). Because i13 arrays hold f64 only, parallel 1-D arrays are exactly the right shape - no struct type needed; the pair want is avoidable here.
spheres.blurb: The smooth curve behind every font glyph, vector drawing, and animation ease, drawn by de Casteljau's algorithm: nothing but repeated linear interpolation between control points - lerp each adjacent pair with ratio t, then lerp the results, a shrinking triangular cascade that collapses to the single point on the curve (and, read sideways, splits the curve in two at t). Its two names honour TWO DIFFERENT MEN: Paul de Casteljau (Citroen, 1959) invented the algorithm but Citroen locked it away as a trade secret and forbade him to publish, while Pierre Bezier (Renault, early 1960s) reached the same curves independently using control VECTORS (not the draggable control points everyone now uses, which are closer to de Casteljau's 'poles') and was allowed to patent and publish (UNISURF, 1968) - so the curve is 'Bezier' and the algorithm is 'de Casteljau', who had it first and lost the eponym to a secrecy policy. The real mathematical root is Sergei Bernstein's basis polynomials (1912, decades before any CAD); A. R. Forrest (1972) spotted that Bezier's curves ARE the Bernstein basis; de Casteljau finally published his own account ('Formes a poles') only in 1985. Note de Casteljau's algorithm is the STABLE, geometrically transparent method, not the fastest (Horner on the Bernstein form is O(n)). In real I-13 it is a strict no-wall: pure f64 lerp, with the (x,y) control points held as two parallel f64 arrays (sidestepping the PS-014 pair want) that the cascade overwrites in place - verified (2.0, 2.25) for the cubic at t=0.5.

spheres.title: MST BY PRIM / JARNIK
spheres.credit: Vojtech Jarnik (1930, published in Czech and overlooked) had the grow-one-tree MST method FIRST; Robert C. Prim (Bell Labs, 1957) and Edsger Dijkstra (1959) each rediscovered it independently - fairly the Jarnik-Prim-Dijkstra algorithm, the earliest inventor getting the smallest share of the name. Otakar Boruvka (1926) gave the first MST algorithm of any kind, a different edge-contracting parallel method, to electrify Moravia
spheres.source: Jarnik 1930 (Czech); Prim, Bell System Technical Journal 36, 1957; Dijkstra, Numerische Mathematik 1, 1959; Boruvka 1926
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - it runs on exactly Dijkstra's (dart 055) array skeleton: key[v] = the cheapest edge into the growing tree (init 0 at the start vertex, +inf elsewhere), inMST[v] = a 0/1 flag, parent[v] = the tree vertex it attaches to (an exact f64 vertex index). Each of the V rounds does a LINEAR scan over key[] for the minimum not-yet-in-tree vertex, marks it, and relaxes its neighbours - O(V^2), NO heap needed, which is the dart's point and optimal for dense graphs (verified MST weight 16 on a 5-vertex graph). The graph itself wants a 2-D weight matrix (PS-004), here flattened to W[i*V+j]; a heap would drop it to O((V+E) log V) via heap-on-array (PS-005, closed by dart 062) - neither is needed for the clean build.
spheres.blurb: A minimum spanning tree connects every vertex at the least total edge cost; this method grows a SINGLE tree from any start, repeatedly pulling in the vertex reachable by the cheapest single edge, then relaxing its neighbours' keys - after V steps the tree spans everything. It is universally called Prim's, but Vojtech Jarnik published it in 1930 (in Czech, so the West missed it), 27 years before Robert Prim rediscovered it at Bell Labs in 1957, and Dijkstra rediscovered it a third time in 1959 - fairly the Jarnik-Prim-Dijkstra algorithm, with the earliest inventor getting the smallest share of the name. (Otakar Boruvka gave the first MST algorithm of any kind back in 1926, a different edge-contracting parallel method, to electrify Moravia efficiently.) The plain version scans for the minimum LINEARLY - O(V^2), no heap - which is optimal for dense graphs. In real I-13 it runs on the very array skeleton Dijkstra (dart 055) uses: key[], inMST[], parent[] as bounded arrays and a linear min-scan (verified MST weight 16); the weight graph wants a 2-D matrix (PS-004), flattened here to W[i*V+j], and a heap (PS-005, closed by 062) would only be needed for sparse graphs.

spheres.title: THE BLOSSOM ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: Jack Edmonds (1965, 'Paths, Trees, and Flowers') gave the blossom-shrinking algorithm for maximum matching in general graphs AND the paper is where computer science first articulated that 'polynomial-time = good/tractable' (the intuition behind the class P). Claude Berge (1957) gave the augmenting-path characterization (a matching is maximum iff no augmenting path); Micali & Vazirani (1980) reached O(sqrt(V) E)
spheres.source: Edmonds, 'Paths, Trees, and Flowers', Canadian J. Math. 17, 1965; Berge 1957 (augmenting paths); Micali & Vazirani 1980
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new for the substrate - match[], parent[], base[] are bounded integer arrays and the whole algorithm is array reads/writes plus recursion (verified: the odd 5-cycle C5 has maximum matching 2, one vertex always left out). The BLOSSOM contraction is index bookkeeping - relabel an odd cycle's vertices to a shared base, find the augmenting path, then unfold - not a new value kind, the move bipartite matching never needs. The honest wall is the same one the trees hit: a rich adjacency structure wants real linked nodes (PS-015) or a 2-D array (PS-004); the flattened edge-list / parallel-array form runs today.
spheres.blurb: Maximum matching in a general graph - pair up as many vertices as possible, no vertex twice - is easy in bipartite graphs by augmenting paths, but ODD CYCLES break the simple approach. Jack Edmonds' 1965 trick is to SHRINK each odd cycle (a 'blossom') into a single node, find the augmenting path in the smaller graph, then expand it back. The paper, 'Paths, Trees, and Flowers', is historically enormous for a second reason: it is where computer science first argued that a 'good' algorithm is a POLYNOMIAL-TIME one - the intuition behind the complexity class P - so before this paper 'solvable' had no agreed cost and after it tractability had a definition. Claude Berge (1957) had given the augmenting-path characterization (a matching is maximum iff it has no augmenting path); Micali and Vazirani (1980) later reached O(sqrt(V) E), faster but the same idea. In real I-13 the matching runs on integer arrays - match[], parent[], base[] - with the blossom contraction as index bookkeeping (relabel a cycle to a shared base), no new value kind (verified: C5's maximum matching is 2 edges); the honest wall is the same rich-adjacency want (PS-015 linked nodes or PS-004 2-D array) the tree darts hit, and the flattened edge-list form runs today.

spheres.title: HOUSEHOLDER QR
spheres.credit: Alston Householder (1958) introduced the reflection-based QR, numerically backward-stable where classical Gram-Schmidt (Erhard Schmidt 1907, Jorgen Gram 1883, and Laplace had the orthogonalization already by 1820) loses orthogonality. The sign choice - aim at -sign(x1)||x||, not + - is the stability detail Wilkinson made famous; Givens rotations zero one entry at a time, Householder a whole sub-column
spheres.source: Householder, 'Unitary Triangularization of a Nonsymmetric Matrix', J. ACM 5(4), 1958; Schmidt 1907; Gram 1883; Laplace (supplements to TAP, ~1820); Wilkinson (rounding-error analysis)
spheres.i13_recommend: the reflection RUNS on the real compiler: dot products (a multiply-add loop over the array), the norm via the stdlib sqrt (or Newton isqrt then reciprocal), forming v = x - alpha*e1, and applying H as a RANK-1 update x' = x - 2*(v^T x / v^T v)*v so the n-by-n matrix is never built (O(n) per column, verified Hx=[-5,0] for x=[3,4], diagonal -> -||x|| = -5). The wall is the MATRIX itself - PS-004, the 2-D array want - hand-flattened row-major idx = r*ncols + c, a third concrete case after Smith-Waterman/knapsack/Hungarian. The sign choice must be coded explicitly (aim at -||x||); the compiler will NOT catch the classic Wilkinson instability bug - a place where the language trusts the author. Only the real case runs (no complex/Hermitian type; f64 only).
spheres.blurb: To factor a matrix into an orthogonal Q and an upper-triangular R - the stable heart of least-squares fitting and eigenvalue solvers - Householder reflects each column so that everything below the diagonal becomes ZERO in one stroke, using the mirror H = I - 2 v v^T / (v^T v). It is a mirror, not the slow one-vector-at-a-time orthogonalization, and it is far more numerically stable: classical Gram-Schmidt (Erhard Schmidt 1907, though Jorgen Gram 1883 and Laplace (by 1820) preceded the name) progressively LOSES orthogonality, while Householder's reflections are backward-stable, which is why dense QR solvers actually run them. Alston Householder introduced it in 1958. The crucial detail is the SIGN choice: aim the reflection at -sign(x1)||x||, not +, to avoid catastrophic cancellation - the instability Wilkinson made famous - and getting it wrong silently degrades the whole factorization. Givens rotations zero one entry at a time; Householder zeros a whole column. In real I-13 the reflection runs entirely on f64 primitives the compiler has - dot products, a norm via sqrt/isqrt, and a rank-1 apply that never materializes the n-by-n matrix (verified Hx = [-5, 0] for x = [3,4]); the wall is the matrix itself, PS-004, hand-flattened row-major, a third concrete motivator for the 2-D-array want alongside Smith-Waterman, knapsack and Hungarian, and the sign choice is the author's to get right (the compiler cannot catch it).

spheres.title: ASYMMETRIC NUMERAL SYSTEMS
spheres.credit: Jarek Duda (2009, formalized ~2013) - a single-state entropy coder that is BOTH near-optimal and Huffman-fast, dissolving the old tradeoff between Huffman (dart 006, whole-bit, fast but lossy-in-bits) and arithmetic coding (optimal but slow and patent-encumbered). Duda placed it in the PUBLIC DOMAIN; Google's rANS-variant application was rejected by the USPTO in 2018 as obvious over his prior art. Now the default entropy stage in zstd (Facebook), LZFSE (Apple), JPEG XL, and CRAM genomics
spheres.source: J. Duda, 'Asymmetric numeral systems', arXiv 2009/2013; zstd, LZFSE, JPEG XL implementations; Google rANS patent application rejected 2018-2019
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new for the tabled (tANS) form - a single integer STATE plus, per symbol, integer multiply/divide/mod and lookups into a bounded frequency/cumulative table, all small integers well inside f64's exact-integer range (< 2^53), so i13's array-of-f64 holds the tables EXACTLY (verified round-trip: enc('b',7)=31, dec(31) -> 'b' with state restored to 7; enc('a',7)=9, the common symbol growing the state less, about 0.42 bits vs the rare symbol's 2 bits, matching -log2(p)). It dissolves Huffman's (dart 006) whole-bit tradeoff on the same integer-array substrate. THE WALL is in streaming rANS, whose growing state must be RENORMALIZED (emit bytes when it crosses a bound) to stay bounded - drop renormalization and the single state climbs past f64's 2^53 ceiling and loses exactness; a fixed-width integer state plus a renormalize primitive is the honest addition, which bounded tANS does not need.
spheres.blurb: For decades, entropy coding forced a choice: Huffman (dart 006) is fast but wastes a fraction of a bit per symbol because it rounds each code to a whole number of bits, while arithmetic coding hits the Shannon limit but is slow and was long patent-encumbered. Asymmetric Numeral Systems (ANS) dissolves the tradeoff - near-optimal ratio at Huffman speed - by folding the whole message into ONE growing integer STATE: encoding a symbol replaces the state with a larger value chosen from the symbol's frequency, and the rarer the symbol the more the state grows, by exactly -log2(p) bits; decoding reads the state's residue to recover the symbol and shrink it back. It is a rare RECENT invention - Jarek Duda formalized it in 2009 (not some pre-1990 classic) - and one Duda deliberately kept patent-free, placing it in the public domain, so that Google's rANS-variant application (filed ~2016) was rejected by the USPTO in 2018 as obvious over his prior art. It is now the default modern entropy stage inside zstd (Facebook), LZFSE (Apple), JPEG XL, and CRAM. In real I-13 the tabled (tANS) form is squarely in the integer-array wheelhouse: a single state plus per-symbol multiply/divide/mod and small-table lookups, all exact in f64 (verified round-trip 7 -> 31 -> 7, common symbols growing the state less); the wall appears only in streaming rANS, whose state must be renormalized to stay under 2^53 - a fixed-width integer state plus a renormalize primitive is the honest want.

spheres.title: THE MARCHING CUBES
spheres.credit: William Lorensen & Harvey Cline (General Electric, SIGGRAPH 1987) - and GE PATENTED it (US 4,710,876, expired 2005), which pushed a generation to marching tetrahedra (developed to circumvent it) - GE's own dividing cubes (US 4,719,585) was itself patented, not an escape. The original 15-case table handled ambiguous faces inconsistently, leaving HOLES/cracks in the mesh (Durst 1988 flagged it, Nielson & Hamann 1991 fixed it with the asymptotic decider); Wyvill's dividing-cubes (1986) is a precedent
spheres.source: Lorensen & Cline, 'Marching Cubes: A High Resolution 3D Surface Construction Algorithm', SIGGRAPH Computer Graphics 21(4), 1987; US Patent 4,710,876; Durst 1988; Nielson & Hamann 1991 (asymptotic decider)
spheres.i13_recommend: the heart RUNS: the corner test compares each corner value < isolevel, shifts the boolean into place with << and ORs the eight into one byte (& | << doing real work, verified cubeindex = 1 for one corner inside), and the vertex interpolation is a plain f64 lerp along each crossed edge (verified edge-t = 0.5). The 256-length edge/case table is a BOUNDED ARRAY lookup - the canonical i13 win. THE STRAIN: the triangulation table is genuinely a 256x16 grid of small INTEGER edge-ids, and i13 arrays hold f64 ONLY (2-D is still a want, PS-004), so it flattens to a length-4096 f64 array with -1 sentinels rounded on read - it works, but the natural 2-D int table is exactly the unmet 2-D-array frontier. The original table's ambiguity bug is the corpus's recurring lesson: an unstated invariant (consistent face resolution) a checker never enforced.
spheres.blurb: To turn a 3-D scalar field (a CT scan, a density function) into a triangle mesh, march a cube through it: classify the 8 corners as inside/outside the surface into an 8-bit index, look up in a 256-case table which cube edges the surface crosses, and place each vertex by linear interpolation along its edge. Simple and fast - and for 18 years PATENTED. William Lorensen and Harvey Cline published it at SIGGRAPH 1987, and General Electric patented it (US 4,710,876), so a whole generation used marching tetrahedra (developed expressly to circumvent the claim) purely to dodge it until the patent expired in 2005 - GE's own dividing cubes (US 4,719,585) was patented too, no escape. The original table also had a real BUG: it handled ambiguous faces inconsistently, leaving holes in the surface - Durst flagged it in 1988, and Nielson and Hamann fixed it in 1991 with the 'asymptotic decider'. In real I-13 the heart runs clean - the corner test is the integrated bitwise ISA (& | <<, verified cubeindex = 1), the vertex placement is an f64 lerp (edge-t = 0.5), and the case table is a bounded-array lookup; the strain is the 256x16 integer triangulation table, which the f64-only rule forces you to flatten to a length-4096 f64 array with -1 sentinels - the natural 2-D int table is the unmet PS-004 want, and the ambiguity bug is the corpus's recurring 'unstated invariant' lesson.

spheres.title: THE STERN-BROCOT TREE
spheres.credit: Moritz Stern (1858, number theory) and Achille Brocot (1861, a Parisian CLOCKMAKER sizing gear trains) found it independently. The mediant (a+c)/(b+d) - wrong as fraction addition, exactly right as a mediant - generates every positive rational once, in lowest terms; the L/R path run-lengths ARE the continued fraction and climbing to the root is the subtractive Euclidean algorithm (dart 027); reading level by level orders the rationals like the Farey sequence
spheres.source: M. Stern 1858; A. Brocot 1861 (gear ratios); Graham, Knuth & Patashnik, 'Concrete Mathematics' (the modern exposition)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - and pointedly so: where AVL (072), red-black (073), the trie (074) and the k-d tree (078) all hit PS-015 (heap-linked nodes with child pointers i13's scalar/array-of-f64 model cannot express), the Stern-Brocot tree DODGES the pointer wall entirely. The tree is INFINITE yet needs ZERO stored nodes: a node's identity IS its L/R address, computed not stored, so at any moment you hold only four integers - the numerator/denominator of the two bracket fractions - and compute each child mediant (a+c)/(b+d) on the fly, choosing L or R by a single comparison against the target (verified path to 3/5 = L R L at depth 4, mediants 1/1 -> 1/2 -> 2/3 -> 3/5, continued fraction [0;1,1,2]). It runs on plain scalars - no allocation, no pointers, no rotations - and ties Euclid (dart 027) directly: the path's run-lengths give the continued fraction (the last run one short of the final term) and the parent is one subtraction step. The only thing that reintroduces the wall is materializing a whole LEVEL in sorted order; for point queries and best-rational-approximation the corpus needs no node objects at all.
spheres.blurb: The Stern-Brocot tree is a binary tree that contains every positive fraction in lowest terms exactly once, built by taking MEDIANTS: bracket a target between two fractions (start 0/1 and 1/0), and their mediant (numerators added, denominators added) is the node between them - compare it to the target, step left or right, and tighten the bracket. It was found independently by Moritz Stern (1858, in number theory) and Achille Brocot (1861), a Parisian CLOCKMAKER who needed it to choose gear ratios - the best rational approximation with small teeth counts. The mediant (a+c)/(b+d) is the wrong way to ADD fractions but exactly right as a mediant, and it generates every rational once, already reduced. The astonishing part for this corpus is that it needs NO stored nodes: a node's identity IS its left/right address, computed on the fly, so you navigate an infinite tree holding only four integers. The path's L/R run-lengths GIVE the fraction's continued fraction (the last run one short of the final term), and climbing back to the root is the subtractive Euclidean algorithm (dart 027) - so 3/5 = [0;1,1,2] has path L R L. In real I-13 this DODGES the pointer wall (PS-015) that sinks AVL/red-black/trie/k-d: it runs on plain scalars with a mediant plus one comparison per step (verified path to 3/5 at depth 4), no allocation or pointers, and ties Euclid directly - the win is for point queries and approximation, not for storing the structure.

spheres.title: THE CYK ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: Three INDEPENDENT inventors - John Cocke (~1960, never published, circulated in lecture notes), Tadao Kasami (1965, a USAF technical report), Daniel Younger (1967, published) - plus Itiroo Sakai (1961); the name 'CYK' is the conventional listing (the ordered name is the alternate CKY: Cocke, Kasami, Younger, both alphabetically and chronologically), NOT by priority - Cocke was first but you would not know it from CYK. O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space general CFG parser requiring Chomsky Normal Form
spheres.source: J. Cocke ~1960 (unpublished lecture notes); T. Kasami 1965 (USAF technical report); D. Younger 1967 (Information and Control 10); I. Sakai 1961
spheres.i13_recommend: the DP RUNS: the outer triangular loops over length then start, the inner split loop over k, the CNF combine (for each rule X->YZ, AND that Y is present in the left cell and Z in the right, then OR X into the result), and the acceptance test all execute on the compiler. A cell's SET of nonterminals packs into one f64 as a BITMASK (S=1, A=2, B=4, C=8), so union is | and membership is & (verified top cell {S,A,C} = 11 for the string 'baaba', ACCEPTED because the start symbol S is present). The table is a 2-D triangular array - PS-004 - flattened by hand to a 1-D f64 array indexed i*(n+1)+l, the same trick as Viterbi (080) and knapsack (053). The only want is a native SET/union type; the bitmask is the honest workaround for a bounded nonterminal alphabet, and this dart's CNF grammar and parser tie straight to I-13's own grammar/parser front end.
spheres.blurb: Given a context-free grammar, does a string belong to the language, and how does it parse? CYK answers with dynamic programming over a TRIANGULAR table: put the grammar in Chomsky Normal Form (rules X->YZ or X->a), fill the bottom row with which symbols make each single letter, then for each longer substring try every split point - if some rule X->YZ has Y making the left part and Z making the right, X makes the whole - building up until the top cell spans the string; if it holds the start symbol, accept. It has THREE independent inventors: John Cocke had it around 1960 but never published it (it circulated in lecture notes), Tadao Kasami reached it in a 1965 USAF technical report, and Daniel Younger published it in 1967 - plus Itiroo Sakai (1961) - and 'CYK' is the conventional listing - NOT by priority (Cocke was first) and NOT alphabetical (the ordered name is the alternate CKY: Cocke, Kasami, Younger, which is chronological order too), so the first inventor is buried in the acronym. It is O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space, and requires Chomsky Normal Form - the price of parsing ANY grammar, ambiguous ones included. In real I-13 the DP runs: the triangular loops, the split loop, and the CNF combine all execute, with each cell's SET of nonterminals packed into one f64 as a bitmask (union = |, membership = &), verified top cell {S,A,C} for 'baaba' and accepted because S is present; the table is a 2-D array (PS-004) flattened i*(n+1)+l exactly like Viterbi (080) and knapsack (053), and the only want is a native set/union type.

spheres.title: BACKPROPAGATION
spheres.credit: Seppo Linnainmaa (1970, MSc thesis, Helsinki) first DESCRIBED the modern reverse mode of automatic differentiation - but for ROUNDING ERROR, with no neural nets; Paul Werbos (1974 PhD / explicit 1982) first tied it to neural nets; Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams (1986, Nature) POPULARIZED it (a rediscovery that showed it learns hidden representations) - Hinton did NOT invent it. The chain rule is Leibniz 1676; gradient descent (the learning STEP, not backprop) is Cauchy 1847; Kelley 1960/Bryson 1961 had it in optimal control; Rosenblatt coined 'back-propagating error' 1962 for a DIFFERENT scheme
spheres.source: Linnainmaa 1970 (MSc thesis, Univ. of Helsinki); Werbos 1974 (Harvard PhD 'Beyond Regression') / 1982; Rumelhart, Hinton & Williams, Nature 323:533-536, 1986; Schmidhuber's deep-learning credit history
spheres.i13_recommend: the arithmetic RUNS - the forward pass is weighted sums (f64 multiply/add) into a nonlinearity, the backward pass is a product of local derivatives; the single-neuron case is pure scalars and executes with no wall, verified dL/dw = 0.14628025 for x=1,w=0.5,b=0,t=0 (sigmoid via std/exp.i13). The one transcendental is the nonlinearity (sigmoid needs exp; the stdlib Taylor supplies it, or swap ReLU = max, no exp). A real net's weight matrices are 2-D = PS-004, flattened to 1-D f64 arrays. Backprop supplies only the GRADIENT; the learning is gradient descent (Cauchy) stepping the weights - two pieces the popular story fuses into one.
spheres.blurb: Backpropagation is how a neural net figures out which way to nudge each weight to reduce error: a FORWARD pass runs the input through the layers (weighted sums squashed through a nonlinearity) and computes a loss, then a BACKWARD pass sweeps from the loss back to the inputs applying the calculus CHAIN RULE to get every weight's gradient - and the clever part is bookkeeping, reusing shared sub-results so ALL the gradients cost about one forward pass. It is literally the chain rule run backward through a computation graph, i.e. the reverse mode of automatic differentiation, and it is NOT the learning rule (that is gradient descent, which consumes the gradients). The credit is badly compressed: the algorithm is Seppo Linnainmaa's 1970 MSc thesis (reverse-mode AD with code, but for rounding-error accumulation, no neural nets), first tied to neural nets by Paul Werbos (proposed in his 1974 thesis; the explicit NN application follows in 1982), and only POPULARIZED by Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams in their 1986 Nature paper - a rediscovery that made it famous, not the first description; Hinton did not invent it, and the '1986' date is really the Nature publication of 1985 work. The chain rule is Leibniz (1676), gradient descent is Cauchy (1847), the chained-gradient idea was born in 1960s optimal control (Kelley, Bryson), and Rosenblatt even coined 'back-propagating error' in 1962 for a different scheme. In real I-13 the arithmetic runs - the single sigmoid neuron gives dL/dw = 0.14628025 exactly (sigmoid via std/exp); the nonlinearity's exp is the one transcendental (or use ReLU = max), and a real net's weight matrices are the PS-004 2-D want, flattened. Every autograd today (PyTorch, TensorFlow) is Linnainmaa's 1970 reverse mode at scale.

spheres.title: THE HOPFIELD NETWORK
spheres.credit: John Hopfield (1982) added the ENERGY FUNCTION (borrowed from spin-glass/Ising physics), proving recall converges, and revived neural nets - winning a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics (with Hinton) - but recurrent associative-memory networks predate him: Shun-ichi Amari (1972) and William Little (1974); the learning rule is Hebb's (1949, 'cells that fire together wire together')
spheres.source: Hopfield, PNAS 79:2554, 1982; Amari 1972; Little 1974; Hebb 1949; 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics (Hopfield & Hinton)
spheres.i13_recommend: almost entirely runnable - state s is a 1-D +/-1 f64 array; the symmetric zero-diagonal weight matrix is 2-D = PS-004, flattened to W[i*N+j]. STORE is a Hebbian outer product (W[i*N+j] += s_i*s_j, f64 multiply-add), RECALL's field h_i = sum_j W[i*N+j]*s_j is an f64 dot product, and the update s_i = sign(h_i) is a single COMPARISON (verified: flip bit 1 of a stored pattern, h_1 = 3 -> sign +1 heals it, energy drops 0 -> -6, the global minimum -1/2(N^2-N) = -6). No new primitive; only the 2-D matrix (PS-004) is a want, here index arithmetic.
spheres.blurb: A Hopfield network stores patterns in a web of symmetric weights; show it a CORRUPTED version and it settles - neuron by neuron, always DOWNHILL in energy - into the nearest stored pattern, an associative memory built straight from physics (it is the Ising model of a magnet, run as recall). Weights store patterns by a Hebbian outer product; recall repeatedly sets each neuron to the sign of its weighted input, and the energy E = -1/2 sum_ij W_ij s_i s_j only ever decreases, so the state slides into a stored pattern. Credit: John Hopfield (1982) contributed the ENERGY FUNCTION - borrowed from spin-glass physics - which proved convergence and made the idea click, reviving neural-net research and winning him a share of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics (with Geoffrey Hinton); but the recurrent associative-memory network itself predates him by a decade, in Shun-ichi Amari (1972) and William Little (1974), and the learning rule is Donald Hebb's (1949). In real I-13 it is almost entirely runnable: state is a 1-D +/-1 f64 array, the weight matrix is the PS-004 2-D want flattened to W[i*N+j], store is an outer-product multiply-add, recall is a dot product, and the update s_i = sign(h_i) is a single comparison (verified h_1 = 3 heals a flipped bit, energy 0 -> -6 the global minimum) - no new primitive, only the 2-D matrix is a want.

spheres.title: FLOYD-WARSHALL
spheres.credit: Bernard Roy (1959, in French) published the transitive-closure algorithm FIRST, overlooked; Stephen Warshall (1962, closure) and Robert Floyd (1962, shortest paths, adapting Warshall) reached it independently - fairly the Roy-Floyd-Warshall algorithm; the algebra is Kleene's (1956, automaton-to-regex). O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space, handles negative edges (but not negative cycles)
spheres.source: B. Roy 1959; S. Warshall, J. ACM 9(1), 1962; R. Floyd, CACM 5(6):345, 1962; S. Kleene 1956
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the matrix is 2-D (PS-004), flattened to d[i*n+j], and the update d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k]+d[k][j]) over each intermediate k is min + add (verified all-pairs distances d[0][2]=4, d[0][3]=6, d[1][3]=3 on a 4-vertex weighted digraph). The transitive-closure form is the BITWISE variant (d[i][j] = d[i][j] OR (d[i][k] AND d[k][j])), which the integrated & | handle. It is the all-pairs corner of the same family as Bellman-Ford (046, one source, negative edges) and Dijkstra (055, one source, non-negative) - and the same six lines are closure, shortest paths, AND regex-from-automaton.
spheres.blurb: Floyd-Warshall answers ALL-PAIRS reachability or shortest paths in one triple loop: for every possible MIDDLE vertex k, ask whether routing each pair (i,j) through k improves it - d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k]+d[k][j]) for shortest paths, or OR/AND for transitive closure. Six lines, a 2-D table, O(n^3) time, and unlike Dijkstra it handles negative edges (just not negative cycles). The credit is a four-name tangle: Bernard Roy published the transitive-closure method in 1959 (in French, so it was overlooked), three years before Stephen Warshall (closure, 1962) and Robert Floyd (shortest paths, adapting Warshall, 1962) reached it - both independently of Roy, though Floyd built on Warshall - fairly the Roy-Floyd-Warshall algorithm - and the underlying algebra is Kleene's (1956, converting a finite automaton to a regular expression is this same closure). In real I-13 it is nothing new: the matrix is the PS-004 2-D want flattened to d[i*n+j], the update is min + add (verified d[0][2]=4, d[0][3]=6, d[1][3]=3), and the transitive-closure form is the bitwise variant the integrated & | handle - one algorithm wearing three hats (closure, shortest paths, regex-from-automaton).

spheres.title: SHAMIR'S SECRET SHARING
spheres.credit: Adi Shamir (1979, 'How to Share a Secret', CACM; the S in RSA) gave the polynomial threshold scheme - and George Blakley (1979) independently gave a GEOMETRIC threshold scheme the SAME year. It is information-theoretically secure: any k-1 shares leave every possible secret equally likely, so no computing power helps. Reconstruction is Lagrange interpolation (dart 100) at x=0 over a finite field
spheres.source: A. Shamir, 'How to Share a Secret', CACM 22(11):612, 1979; G. Blakley, AFIPS 1979 (geometric threshold); Lagrange interpolation
spheres.i13_recommend: the tiny demo RUNS end-to-end on the merged modular % plus a modular inverse from extended Euclid (dart 084): building f(x) = S + a*x (mod 13), evaluating the shares, and reconstructing S = f(0) by Lagrange at x=0 are all exact integer operations in a small prime field (verified: secret S=7, shares (1,12),(2,4),(3,9), rebuild S=7 from ANY 2 of the 3, and the one division uses (-2)^-1 = 6 mod 13 from extended Euclid; inv(2)=7 mod 13) - no floating point. THE WALL: real deployments use a 128- or 256-bit prime, so every coefficient, share value, and Lagrange product needs BIGNUM (dart 050's addition); the toy field runs in f64, the real field is a clean bignum job.
spheres.blurb: Shamir's secret sharing splits a secret into n SHARES so that any k of them rebuild it and any k-1 reveal NOTHING at all: hide the secret as the constant term of a random degree-(k-1) polynomial, hand out points (i, f(i)) as shares; k points fix the polynomial uniquely (so k shares recover f(0)=S by Lagrange interpolation), while k-1 points fit infinitely many polynomials, leaving every secret equally likely. It is information-theoretically secure - not merely hard but IMPOSSIBLE to break under-threshold, no computing power helps. Adi Shamir (the S in RSA) published it in 1979 ('How to Share a Secret'), and George Blakley published a different, geometric threshold scheme (the secret is a point where k hyperplanes meet) the SAME year, 1979, independently. In real I-13 the tiny demo runs end-to-end on the merged modular % plus a modular inverse from extended Euclid (dart 084): with secret 7 and shares (1,12),(2,4),(3,9) over GF(13), reconstruction from any two shares gives 7 exactly (and inv(2)=7 mod 13), no floating point; the wall is only scale - a real 256-bit prime makes every share and Lagrange product a bignum job (dart 050's addition).

spheres.title: FORTUNE'S ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: Steven Fortune (1986) gave the elegant SWEEPLINE (a 'beach line' of parabolas), the same O(n log n) but simpler to implement - but the O(n log n) BOUND is Shamos & Hoey (1975, divide-and-conquer), and the Voronoi diagram itself is centuries old: Descartes (1644), Dirichlet (1850), Georgy Voronoy (1908); its dual is the Delaunay triangulation (Delaunay 1934)
spheres.source: S. Fortune, 'A sweepline algorithm for Voronoi diagrams', Algorithmica 2, 1987 (ACM SoCG 1986); Shamos & Hoey 1975; G. Voronoy 1908; B. Delaunay 1934
spheres.i13_recommend: the arithmetic core RUNS: the parabola breakpoints and the circle-event CIRCUMCENTER are pure f64 (verified the Voronoi vertex where the three regions of sites (0,0),(4,0),(1,3) meet is the circumcenter (2,1), equidistant at radius sqrt(5)), and the event priority queue is exactly a binary min-heap on an f64 array keyed by sweep coordinate (PS-005, closed by dart 062). The strain is the BEACH LINE: a balanced ordered structure of arcs - the pointer wall (PS-015), the same one the search trees hit. The simplest correct Voronoi (nearest-site colouring, O(n) per pixel) needs nothing at all; Fortune is the fast build, and only its beach line reaches past the array.
spheres.blurb: A Voronoi diagram carves the plane into the region nearest each site - the map behind 'which store is closest', mesh generation, and nature's cracked patterns - and Fortune's algorithm builds it in O(n log n) by sweeping a line down the plane while tracking a 'beach line' of parabolas (each site's set of points equidistant from it and the sweep line), whose breakpoints trace the Voronoi edges: SITE events add arcs, CIRCLE events remove one and fix a Voronoi vertex. Credit: Steven Fortune (1986) gave this elegant sweepline, but the O(n log n) BOUND was already Shamos and Hoey's (1975, by divide-and-conquer), and the diagram itself is centuries old - Descartes sketched it (1644), Dirichlet studied it (1850), and Georgy Voronoy gave the general treatment (1908); its dual is the Delaunay triangulation (Delaunay 1934). In real I-13 the arithmetic core runs cleanly: the parabola breakpoints and the circle-event circumcenter are f64 (verified the vertex of sites (0,0),(4,0),(1,3) is the circumcenter (2,1), radius sqrt(5)), and the event queue is a binary heap on an f64 array (PS-005, closed by dart 062); the strain is the beach line, a balanced ordered arc structure - the PS-015 pointer wall - while the simplest correct Voronoi (nearest-site colouring) needs nothing at all.

spheres.title: HIERHOLZER'S ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: Leonhard Euler (1736, Seven Bridges of Konigsberg) PROVED the even-degree condition - and FOUNDED graph theory (prefiguring topology) - but gave NO constructive algorithm; Carl Hierholzer (1873, published posthumously - he died 1871, aged 30) gave the walk-and-splice algorithm in linear time; Fleury (1883) gave the more famous but SLOWER O(E^2) rule ('never cross a bridge you cannot come back over')
spheres.source: L. Euler, 'Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis', 1736; C. Hierholzer 1873 (posthumous); Fleury 1883
spheres.i13_recommend: the EXISTENCE TEST runs cleanly - a degree-parity scan (an integer-count array indexed by vertex, checked all-even in O(V+E), verified ok=1 for a 5-vertex Euler-circuit graph and ok=0 for Konigsberg's degrees 3,3,3,5). ONE MILD WALL: the CONNECTIVITY half of the condition is not a pure array scan - it needs a traversal (DFS/BFS over an adjacency array), because two even-degree components pass the parity test yet have no single circuit. CONSTRUCTION (Hierholzer) runs on arrays exactly as the angle says: a boolean edge-used flag array, a per-vertex 'next unused edge' index, and an explicit stack of vertices - the splice is a stack operation, the corpus's home turf, not the pointer wall the search trees hit.
spheres.blurb: Can you walk a graph using EVERY edge exactly once and return to start (an Euler circuit)? Euler answered WHEN in 1736 - the graph must be connected and every vertex must have even degree - solving the Seven Bridges of Konigsberg (whose four landmasses have odd degree, so no such walk exists) and in the process FOUNDING graph theory and prefiguring topology. But Euler gave only the CRITERION, not a method; Carl Hierholzer gave the algorithm in 1873 (published posthumously - he had died in 1871 aged 30): walk unused edges until you return to start (a closed loop), then if any vertex on it still has unused edges, walk a new loop from there and SPLICE it in, repeating until no edge is left - linear time. (Fleury's 1883 rule, 'never cross a bridge you cannot come back over', is more famous but slower, O(E^2).) In real I-13 the existence test runs cleanly as a degree-parity scan (verified ok=1 for a 5-vertex graph, ok=0 for Konigsberg's 3,3,3,5); the one mild wall is that the connectivity half needs a traversal (DFS over an adjacency array), not a pure scan; and Hierholzer's construction runs on a boolean edge-used array plus an explicit stack - the splice is a stack operation, the corpus's home turf, not the pointer wall.
spheres.kicker: dart 099 - a helldive at the net

spheres.title: LAGRANGE INTERPOLATION
spheres.credit: Edward Waring (1779) PUBLISHED the interpolation formula 16 years before Joseph-Louis Lagrange (1795); Euler had it too (1783) - fairly 'Waring-Lagrange'; Newton's divided differences (~1675) give the same unique polynomial in an incrementally-better form. Caution: high-degree interpolation on evenly-spaced points oscillates wildly at the ends (Runge's phenomenon, 1901) - more points is not always better
spheres.source: E. Waring, Phil. Trans. Royal Soc., 1779; J.-L. Lagrange 1795; L. Euler 1783; I. Newton ~1675 (divided differences); C. Runge 1901 (the phenomenon)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - evaluating the interpolant L(x*) = sum_i y_i * prod_{j!=i} (x*-x_j)/(x_i-x_j) at a fixed target is pure multiply/divide/add, so it runs directly on i13's f64 array machine (verified P(3)=13 through points (0,1),(1,3),(2,7), which reproduces the underlying quadratic x^2+x+1 because 3 points determine a unique degree-<=2 polynomial). It is the EXACT engine behind Shamir secret sharing (097): reconstructing the secret is Lagrange interpolation of the share-polynomial at x=0. The one wall is Shamir's, not Lagrange's - 'over a field' means exact modular integers (GF(p)) which f64 cannot hold, so the cryptographic version needs bignum; the real-number interpolation here is pure f64.
spheres.blurb: Given n points there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n-1 through them all, and Lagrange writes it down directly as a blend of BASIS polynomials L_i(x) = prod_{j!=i} (x-x_j)/(x_i-x_j), each worth 1 at its own node x_i and 0 at every other, so the interpolant sum_i y_i L_i(x) hits each y_i because only that basis is alive there. It is the engine behind Shamir's secret sharing (dart 097), numerical integration, and every smooth 'connect the dots'. Credit is a naming accident: Edward Waring published the formula in 1779, sixteen years BEFORE Joseph-Louis Lagrange (1795), and Euler stated it in 1783 - fairly 'Waring-Lagrange' - while Newton's divided differences (~1675) give the same polynomial in a form better for adding points incrementally; Lagrange's clean presentation is simply what stuck to the name. A caution the dart names: high-degree interpolation on evenly-spaced points oscillates wildly at the ends (Runge's phenomenon), so more points is not always better. In real I-13 it is nothing new - the evaluation is multiply/divide/add and runs directly (verified P(3)=13 for the quadratic x^2+x+1) - and it is the exact engine behind Shamir (097); the only wall is Shamir's finite field (GF(p) needs bignum), not the real-number interpolation, which is pure f64.

spheres.title: LLOYD'S ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: Stuart Lloyd (1957, Bell Labs) devised the assign-and-average method for PCM quantization but left it in an INTERNAL MEMO, unpublished until 1982 - so for 25 years it was reinvented by others: Hugo Steinhaus (1956, the continuous version, even earlier), Joseph Max (1960, independently, the 'Lloyd-Max quantizer'), Forgy (1965, the batch form), and James MacQueen (1967, who COINED 'k-means'). It finds a LOCAL optimum (the result depends on the start; k-means++ 2007 seeds better)
spheres.source: S. Lloyd 1957 (Bell Labs memo, publ. IEEE Trans. Info. Theory 1982); H. Steinhaus 1956; J. Max 1960; E. Forgy 1965; J. MacQueen 1967; Arthur & Vassilvitskii 2007 (k-means++)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - hold the points and the centres as parallel f64 arrays xs[]/ys[]; the nearest-centre test is a pure-f64 inner loop dx=xs[i]-sx[j], dy=ys[i]-sy[j], d=dx*dx+dy*dy with a running argmin (NO sqrt needed, since squared distance shares the argmin), and the update is sum-then-divide (accumulate sum_x/sum_y/count per cluster, then sx[j]=sum_x/count). Verified one step on 5 points/2 centres: centroids (5/3, 4/3) and (4.5, 3.5), then a second pass leaves the assignments unchanged (converged). The whole loop is in i13's comfort zone. The points are (x,y) PAIRS - the PS-014 pair want - sidestepped by parallel arrays exactly as Bezier (086); it relaxes the Voronoi diagram Fortune (098) builds - a natural pair.
spheres.blurb: Lloyd's algorithm scatters a few centres among points, then alternates two steps: ASSIGN each point to its nearest centre (a Voronoi partition), and UPDATE each centre to the mean of its assigned points - repeated until the centres stop moving, drifting into evenly-spaced cells (a centroidal Voronoi tessellation). It is EXACTLY the k-means loop, and it relaxes the diagram Fortune (dart 098) builds. The credit is a 25-year burial: Stuart Lloyd devised it at Bell Labs in 1957 for PCM quantization but left it in an internal memo, UNPUBLISHED until 1982, so it was independently reinvented again and again - Hugo Steinhaus had the continuous version even earlier (1956), Joseph Max reached it in 1960 (the 'Lloyd-Max quantizer'), Forgy gave the batch form (1965), and James MacQueen coined the name 'k-means' (1967). It finds only a LOCAL optimum, so the result depends on where the centres start (k-means++ 2007 seeds them better). In real I-13 it is nothing new: hold points and centres as parallel f64 arrays, the nearest-centre test is dx*dx+dy*dy with a running argmin (no sqrt needed), and the update is sum-then-divide (verified one step gives centroids (5/3,4/3) and (4.5,3.5), then stable); the (x,y) pairs are the PS-014 want, sidestepped by parallel arrays exactly as Bezier (086), and it relaxes the Voronoi diagram Fortune (098) builds.

spheres.title: LZ78 DICTIONARY COMPRESSION
spheres.credit: Jacob Ziv & Abraham Lempel (1978) invented the phrase-dictionary scheme (LZ78) - note Ziv is FIRST author yet the eponym flips to 'Lempel-Ziv'. Terry Welch (1984) TUNED it into LZW (pre-load all single chars, emit one index per phrase) and filed a patent WITHOUT disclosing it in his paper; IBM's Miller-Wegman filing beat Welch's by 19 days. GIF (1987) used LZW believing it free; Unisys later demanded licensing (the 1994 'GIF tax'), motivating patent-free PNG (1996, which uses LZ77+Huffman not LZW); the US LZW patent expired 2003
spheres.source: Ziv & Lempel, IEEE Trans. Info. Theory 24(5), 1978 (LZ78); Welch, IEEE Computer 17(6), 1984 (LZW); US patent 4,558,302 (filed 1983, expired 2003); GIF87a 1987; PNG 1.0 1996
spheres.i13_recommend: the numeric spine RUNS on i13's bounded f64 arrays: the index arithmetic and the emit/decode loop, with the dictionary held as a TRIE IN PARALLEL ARRAYS (a parent-index array + an edge-character array as f64 code points). Matching the longest known prefix, appending a new numbered entry, and emitting (index, char) tokens are all bounded-array bookkeeping (verified round-trip: ABABABA -> tokens (0,A)(0,B)(1,B)(3,A), dict 1=A/2=B/3=AB/4=ABA, decodes back exactly). The WALL is the standing string want: the dictionary holds growing STRINGS (with Boyer-Moore-061, KMP-063, BWT-065, the trie-074). Token 4=(3,A) reuses entry 3 built one step earlier - the trie growing on itself is the pointerless node-arena shape the corpus already uses.
spheres.blurb: LZ78 compresses by building a DICTIONARY of phrases as it reads, shipping no table ahead of time: it takes the longest prefix already catalogued (index i), reads the next character c, emits the pair (i, c), and adds 'that phrase + c' as a new numbered entry; the decoder replays the exact same construction, so both sides end with identical dictionaries and nothing extra is transmitted. Credit is doubly tangled. First, the phrase-dictionary idea is Jacob Ziv and Abraham Lempel's (LZ78, 1978, the sibling of their 1977 sliding-window LZ77 that underlies zip/gzip/PNG) - and although Ziv is the FIRST author on both papers, the eponym flips to 'Lempel-Ziv'. Second, Terry Welch's famous LZW (1984) is a TUNED refinement of LZ78, not a new idea - he pre-loaded the dictionary with every single character so each phrase costs one index instead of an (index, char) pair - and he filed a patent without disclosing it in his paper (IBM's Miller-Wegman application actually beat Welch's by 19 days). LZW is what GIF, TIFF and Unix compress use, and when Unisys (which inherited Welch's patent) demanded licensing in 1994 - the 'GIF tax' - it drove the creation of patent-free PNG (which uses LZ77+Huffman, sidestepping LZW) before the patent expired in 2003. In real I-13 the numeric spine runs on bounded arrays - index arithmetic and the emit/decode loop, the dictionary a trie in parallel arrays (verified ABABABA round-trips through tokens (0,A)(0,B)(1,B)(3,A)); the wall is that the dictionary holds growing STRINGS, the standing aggregate want.

spheres.title: THE QR ALGORITHM
spheres.credit: TWO independent inventors: John G. F. Francis (UK, Part I received October 1959) and Vera N. Kublanovskaya (USSR, received February 1961) - Francis was EARLIER, so 'both in 1961 simultaneous' is a publication coincidence, not simultaneous discovery. 'QR' names the QR DECOMPOSITION, not a person. The core idea is Heinz Rutishauser's LR algorithm (1958), itself from his quotient-difference algorithm (1954); QR is the orthogonal (numerically stable) analogue. Named a 'top-10 algorithm of the 20th century'; Francis then left the field and was untraceable for decades
spheres.source: Francis, Computer Journal, Parts I & II 1961/62 (Part I received Oct 1959); Kublanovskaya 1961 (received Feb 1961); Rutishauser LR 1958, qd 1954; Dongarra & Sullivan 'Top Ten Algorithms of the Century'
spheres.i13_recommend: for a real SYMMETRIC input everything is real f64, so the whole loop RUNS: factor A = QR (via Householder reflections, dart 089), form A' = RQ (a similarity, same eigenvalues), test sub-diagonal convergence (sqrt/fabs), and read the eigenvalues off the diagonal - verified the 2x2 [[2,1],[1,2]] converges to diag(3,1). The MATRIX is 2-D = PS-004 (i13 arrays are 1-D f64 only), flattened to A[i*n+j]. The 2x2 closed form (a+d)/2 +/- sqrt(((a-d)/2)^2 + b^2) is exactly what the iteration converges to (the ground truth). A shift gives cubic convergence; unshifted it converges linearly at rate lambda_min/lambda_max.
spheres.blurb: The QR algorithm finds a matrix's EIGENVALUES without ever forming a characteristic polynomial: factor A = QR (orthogonal Q times upper-triangular R, via Householder reflections, dart 089), then remultiply in reverse A' = RQ - which is the similarity Q^T A Q, so the eigenvalues are preserved - and iterate; the sub-diagonal entries shrink and the diagonal converges to the eigenvalues (a 'shift' makes it cubic). It has TWO independent inventors, not one: John Francis in the UK (his Part I was received October 1959) and Vera Kublanovskaya in the USSR (received February 1961) - so the 'both 1961, simultaneous' story is a publication coincidence, and Francis was earlier; fairly the Francis-Kublanovskaya algorithm. 'QR' names the QR decomposition, not a person, and neither inventor originated the core idea - it is the orthogonal, numerically stable analogue of Heinz Rutishauser's 1958 LR algorithm (from his 1954 quotient-difference algorithm). It was named a 'top-10 algorithm of the 20th century', and Francis - who then left the field and was untraceable for decades - built the deflating, shifted form solvers still run. In real I-13 the loop runs entirely in f64 for a symmetric input (verified [[2,1],[1,2]] -> eigenvalues 3, 1); the matrix is the PS-004 2-D want flattened to A[i*n+j], and the 2x2 closed form is the ground truth the iteration approaches.

spheres.title: THE SIMPLEX METHOD
spheres.credit: George B. Dantzig (1947) GENUINELY invented the simplex ALGORITHM - the eponym is CORRECT, do NOT over-correct to Kantorovich. But Leonid Kantorovich (1939, USSR) formulated LINEAR PROGRAMMING (the field) first and independently, unknown in the West for years; and the 1975 Nobel in Economics went to Kantorovich & Koopmans, NOT Dantzig (a famous omission). Klee & Minty (1972) built an input where simplex visits all 2^n corners (exponential worst case, though fast in practice)
spheres.source: Dantzig 1947 (simplex method); Kantorovich 1939 (linear programming); Klee & Minty 1972 (exponential worst case); 1975 Nobel Prize in Economics (Kantorovich & Koopmans)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - the whole inner loop is f64 arithmetic on a TABLEAU (a 2-D array = PS-004, flattened row-major): computing reduced costs, the minimum-ratio test (a divide-and-compare down one column), selecting the entering variable, and the pivot itself (scale the pivot row, subtract multiples from every other row - plain Gaussian elimination). Verified a tiny LP: maximize 3x+5y s.t. x<=4, 2y<=12, 3x+2y<=18 -> optimum (2,6), z=36, path (0,0)->(0,6)->(2,6), two pivots. It is a natural companion to Gauss/Householder (089) - the same row-operation machinery, aimed at optimisation.
spheres.blurb: Linear programming - maximise a linear objective under linear constraints - is the workhorse of planning, logistics and economics, and the simplex method solves it by walking the CORNERS of the feasible polytope: start at a vertex and each pivot moves along an edge to a neighbouring corner that improves the objective, stopping when none does (the optimum is always at a corner). The credit needs care in BOTH directions. The eponym is CORRECT - George Dantzig genuinely invented the simplex algorithm in 1947 - so the common 'over-correction' that hands it to Kantorovich is wrong. But Leonid Kantorovich did formulate linear programming, the FIELD, first (1939, in the USSR, independently and unknown in the West for years), and in a famous omission the 1975 Nobel in Economics went to Kantorovich and Koopmans, NOT to Dantzig. Klee and Minty (1972) built a distorted cube where simplex visits every one of 2^n corners - an exponential worst case - even though it is famously fast in practice, which is precisely why polynomial-time interior-point methods were later sought. In real I-13 it is nothing new: the tableau is the PS-004 2-D want flattened row-major, and every pivot is ratios and Gaussian row operations in f64 (verified max 3x+5y over x<=4, 2y<=12, 3x+2y<=18 -> optimum 36 at (2,6)).

spheres.title: UKKONEN'S SUFFIX TREE
spheres.credit: Ukkonen did NOT invent the first linear-time suffix tree - Peter Weiner did, in 1973 (22 years earlier; Weiner called it a 'bi-tree', built right-to-left; Knuth reportedly called it 'the algorithm of the year'). Edward McCreight (1976) gave the name 'suffix tree', a simpler left-to-right build, AND suffix links. Ukkonen's genuine first (1995) is the ONLINE (prefix-at-a-time) linear-time construction with the 'active point'; suffix links are Weiner/McCreight's, not his
spheres.source: Weiner 1973 ('bi-tree'); McCreight, J. ACM 1976 (the name 'suffix tree' + suffix links); Ukkonen, Algorithmica 1995 (online construction, active point)
spheres.i13_recommend: all the BOOKKEEPING runs on i13's f64 arrays: active-node id, active-edge index into the string, active-length, the remainder counter, the global end variable, and every edge label as a (start,end) pair of integer indices - all f64-representable integers, array-native (verified 'banana' -> 15 distinct substrings, 21 with multiplicity; its suffix tree for banana$ has 7 leaves and 3 internal nodes). The WALL is the suffix TREE itself: nodes with child pointers AND suffix links - PS-015, the pointer wall, shared with AVL (072), red-black (073), the trie (074), the k-d tree (078). The node-arena encoding (children/suffix-link as parallel index arrays) runs today; a first-class linked value is the honest add.
spheres.blurb: A suffix tree indexes EVERY suffix of a string in one structure, so substring search, longest-repeat, and matching become a walk from the root in time proportional to the query, not the text; Ukkonen's 1995 construction builds it left-to-right, ONLINE, in linear time using an 'active point' and suffix links, and is famous for being correct, fast, and very hard to understand. The credit is a made-efficient-vs-first correction: Ukkonen did NOT invent the linear-time suffix tree - Peter Weiner did in 1973, 22 years earlier (Weiner called it a 'bi-tree' and built it right-to-left; Knuth reportedly called it 'the algorithm of the year'), and Edward McCreight (1976) gave both the name 'suffix tree' and the suffix links Ukkonen is often credited with. Ukkonen's real first is the ONLINE (prefix-at-a-time) construction with the active point - the version people teach and implement. A string can have up to Theta(n^2) DISTINCT substrings (banana has 15), yet the suffix tree represents them all with only O(n) nodes - linear space, not a linear count. In real I-13 all the active-point bookkeeping runs on f64 arrays (integer node ids, edge labels as (start,end) index pairs; verified banana -> 15 distinct substrings, tree of 7 leaves and 3 internal nodes); the wall is the suffix TREE itself - nodes with child pointers and suffix links - the PS-015 pointer wall shared with AVL/red-black/trie/k-d, expressible as a node arena.

spheres.title: THE DAVIS-PUTNAM / DPLL
spheres.credit: 'DP' and 'DPLL' are TWO different algorithms, not one. Davis & Putnam (1960) is a RESOLUTION / variable-elimination method - and it ALREADY contains unit propagation (the 'one-literal rule') and pure-literal elimination (the 'affirmative-negative rule'), so those are NOT the 1962 paper's contribution. Davis, Logemann & Loveland (1962) replaced resolution's memory blow-up with BACKTRACKING case-analysis (the splitting rule) - that is DPLL's genuine novelty, and the extra 'LL' marks the different algorithm. SAT is the first NP-complete problem (Cook 1971)
spheres.source: Davis & Putnam, J. ACM 1960 (resolution, one-literal & affirmative-negative rules); Davis, Logemann & Loveland, CACM 1962 (the splitting rule); Cook 1971 (SAT NP-complete); CDCL 1996+
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - a literal is a signed integer (+k = x_k, -k = NOT x_k), a clause a bounded int array, the formula an array of clauses, the partial assignment an int array over {unassigned, true, false}; unit propagation, pure-literal elimination, and the recursive split with backtracking are array scans + integer comparisons + the recursion stack (verified: the formula (-1)(1,2)(-2,3) is SATISFIABLE with (x1,x2,x3)=(false,true,true), and adding (-3) makes it UNSATISFIABLE by conflict at level 0). No new value kind. The whole solve above was FORCED - every assignment a unit propagation, no split needed - which is exactly why unit propagation is the workhorse of real solvers.
spheres.blurb: DPLL decides Boolean satisfiability by backtracking search with two accelerators - unit propagation (a one-literal clause forces its variable) and pure-literal elimination - and is the ancestor of every modern SAT and SMT solver behind hardware verification, planning, and automated reasoning. The name hides that it is really TWO papers, two algorithms. Davis & Putnam (1960) is a RESOLUTION / variable-elimination method - and it already contains the 'one-literal rule' (unit propagation) and the 'affirmative-negative rule' (pure literal), so those are NOT the later paper's idea. Davis, Logemann & Loveland (1962) replaced resolution's memory blow-up with BACKTRACKING case-analysis - the splitting rule - which is DPLL's genuine contribution, and the appended 'LL' precisely marks the different algorithm (DP is resolution, DPLL is search). SAT was the first problem proven NP-complete (Cook 1971), yet DPLL with modern clause learning (CDCL, 1996+) solves industrial instances with millions of variables. In real I-13 it is nothing new: literals are signed integers, clauses and the assignment are bounded int arrays, and unit propagation, pure-literal, and the recursive split are array scans plus the recursion stack (verified (-1)(1,2)(-2,3) is SAT with (false,true,true), UNSAT when (-3) is added) - and that whole solve was forced by unit propagation with no split, which is why unit propagation is the workhorse.

spheres.title: REJECTION SAMPLING
spheres.credit: Rejection sampling was NOT born in the 1951 proceedings - John von Neumann described it in a LETTER to Robert Richtmyer dated 11 March 1947 (published later in the 1951 NBS notes). Three separate credits: von Neumann invented the REJECTION method; the Monte Carlo METHOD was Ulam's 1946 idea (playing solitaire while ill, wondering if random trials estimate the odds); the NAME 'Monte Carlo' was Nicholas Metropolis's (for the casino where Ulam's uncle gambled). The same 1951 paper holds the 'state of sin' quote and the middle-square PRNG - but those are about GENERATING digits, a different topic
spheres.source: von Neumann, letter to Robert Richtmyer 11 March 1947 (publ. NBS Applied Math Series 12, 1951); Ulam 1946 (Monte Carlo); Metropolis (the name 'Monte Carlo')
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - to estimate pi, pull uniform draws x,y in [0,1] from the stdlib seeded LCG and accept a point iff x*x + y*y <= 1.0 (a single f64 comparison, no transcendental), tally accepted/total, report 4*accepted/total. The LCG stream, the accept/reject comparison, the integer tally, and full determinism under a fixed seed all RUN (verified LCG seed 107, N=2000 -> inside=1565, pi ~ 3.13; same seed gives the same estimate bit for bit). It converges only as 1/sqrt(N), the honest catch. It is the twin of Buffon's needle (031) and the whole Monte Carlo family, and determinism-under-a-seed is exactly what a corpus that seals everything to a hash wants.
spheres.blurb: Rejection sampling is the campaign's own metaphor made literal: to sample from a shape or measure an area, throw random points into a bounding box and KEEP only those that land inside - one comparison per point, no formula for the shape needed. To estimate pi, throw points in the unit square and count those inside the quarter-circle (x^2+y^2 <= 1); the fraction times 4 estimates pi. The credit splits three ways and the date is usually wrong: von Neumann described the accept/reject method in a LETTER to Robert Richtmyer (the Los Alamos theory lead) dated 11 March 1947 (not the 1951 proceedings where it was later published); the Monte Carlo METHOD itself was Stanislaw Ulam's 1946 idea (dreamed up playing solitaire while ill); and the NAME 'Monte Carlo' was Nicholas Metropolis's, for the casino where Ulam's uncle gambled. (The same 1951 paper carries von Neumann's 'state of sin' quote and the middle-square PRNG, but those concern generating random digits, a different problem.) In real I-13 it is nothing new: pull uniform x,y from the stdlib seeded LCG, accept iff x^2+y^2 <= 1 (one comparison, no trig), tally, report 4*inside/N (verified seed 107, N=2000 -> pi ~ 3.13, deterministic bit-for-bit under the seed); it converges as 1/sqrt(N), and is the honest twin of Buffon's needle (031) - the dart thrown at the dark, kept if it lands.

spheres.title: EULER'S TOTIENT
spheres.credit: Three different people for the man, the symbol, and the name. Euler defined the function in WORDS in 1763 (E271: 'the multitude of numbers less than N which are prime to N'), with NO symbol; he later (1784) used the letter pi, not phi. The symbol phi is GAUSS's, introduced in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801). The name 'totient' was coined by J. J. Sylvester in 1879 - 116 years after Euler defined the function. It is the secret quantity behind RSA (dart 050): phi(pq) = (p-1)(q-1)
spheres.source: Euler 1763 (E271, in words); Euler 1784 (E564, uses pi); Gauss, Disquisitiones Arithmeticae 1801 (the symbol phi); Sylvester 1879 (the name 'totient')
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - two routes run on i13's integer/bignum machinery: (a) factor n and apply phi(n) = n * prod over distinct primes p|n of (1 - 1/p), each factor n/p*(p-1) staying integral; or (b) count coprimes directly, looping k=1..n and tallying gcd(k,n)=1 via the Euclidean gcd (dart 027), an O(n) scan. Both give phi(36) = 12 and phi(3599) = phi(59*61) = 58*60 = 3480 (verified). For RSA-sized n it wants bignum (dart 050's addition), which the corpus has. It closes the loop with RSA (050): phi is the exact quantity the private exponent is computed against, mod which the encryption inverts.
spheres.blurb: Euler's totient phi(n) counts the integers from 1 to n that share no factor with n; it satisfies phi(n) = n * prod over distinct primes p|n of (1 - 1/p), so phi(36) = 36*(1/2)*(2/3) = 12, and for two primes phi(pq) = (p-1)(q-1). It is a cornerstone of number theory and the SECRET quantity behind RSA (dart 050) - the private key exists precisely because phi(pq) is trivial to compute if you factored n and hopeless if you did not. The credit is three separate people: Euler defined the function in WORDS in 1763 with no symbol at all ('the multitude of numbers less than N and prime to it'), proving what is now Euler's theorem, and he later (1784) used the letter pi for it, NOT phi; the symbol phi is Gauss's, introduced in Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801); and the name 'totient' was coined by J. J. Sylvester in 1879, 116 years after Euler defined the function. In real I-13 it is nothing new - either factor n and apply the product formula, or count coprimes with Euclid's gcd (dart 027, an O(n) scan) - verified phi(36)=12 and phi(3599)=(59-1)(61-1)=3480; RSA-sized n wants bignum, and it closes the loop with RSA (050), phi being the modulus the private exponent inverts against.

spheres.title: THE JACOBI EIGENVALUE SWEEP
spheres.credit: The eponym is CORRECT - Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi (1846, Crelle vol. 30) genuinely invented the rotation-sweep algorithm; do NOT over-correct this one. But Jacobi did NOT invent the eigenvalue problem or the fact that symmetric matrices diagonalize: the 'secular equation' (characteristic equation) comes from Lagrange & Laplace's celestial mechanics (1770s-1780s) - 'secular' is an astronomy word (Latin saeculum, a century) for the slow long-period drift of planetary orbits. The method was rediscovered for computers in the 1950s, prized because each rotation is independent (naturally parallel)
spheres.source: Jacobi 1846 (Crelle vol. 30); the 'secular equation' from Lagrange & Laplace celestial mechanics (1770s-80s); 1950s computer rediscovery (von Neumann era)
spheres.i13_recommend: nothing new - store the symmetric matrix flattened A[i*n+j] (2-D = PS-004, i13 arrays are 1-D f64 only, fine here since every entry is f64); the loop scans all i<j for the largest |a_ij| (an f64 comparison sweep), computes the angle from tan(2theta) = 2*a_pq/(a_pp - a_qq) using cos/sin from the stdlib Taylor (theta = 45 degrees, c=s=sqrt(2)/2 in the equal-diagonal case, needing no atan), and applies the rotation to rows/cols p and q. Verified: [[2,1],[1,2]] diagonalises to diag(3,1) in ONE 45-degree rotation, off-diagonal -> 0. A lovely contrast with QR (103): both find eigenvalues of the same matrix, one by factoring, one by rotating - both on f64. Ties the Jacobi lineage the corpus already carries.
spheres.blurb: To find the eigenvalues of a SYMMETRIC matrix, Jacobi's method repeatedly picks the largest off-diagonal entry and applies a plane ROTATION that zeroes it (angle from tan(2theta) = 2a_ij/(a_ii - a_jj)); each rotation nudges other entries, but the off-diagonal total steadily falls and the diagonal converges to the eigenvalues. It is old (1846), well-suited to parallel hardware (in its cyclic-ordering variant, rotations on disjoint index pairs run concurrently; the classical largest-pivot sweep is sequential), and beautifully simple. This is a rare case where the eponym is exactly RIGHT - Carl Jacobi genuinely invented the rotation sweep, so 'debunking' it would be an over-correction - but the eigenvalue problem itself predates him: the 'secular equation' (the characteristic equation) arose in Lagrange and Laplace's celestial mechanics of the 1770s-80s, where 'secular' is an astronomy word (Latin saeculum, a century) for the slow drift of planetary orbits - and fittingly Jacobi built his method to compute exactly those secular perturbations. The method was rediscovered for computers in the 1950s, prized because each rotation is independent and so naturally parallel. In real I-13 it is nothing new: store the symmetric matrix flattened A[i*n+j] (PS-004), scan for the largest off-diagonal, compute cos/sin from the stdlib Taylor (exactly 45 degrees for equal diagonals), and apply the rotation - verified [[2,1],[1,2]] -> diag(3,1) in one rotation; a lovely contrast with QR (103), both finding eigenvalues of the same matrix, one by factoring and one by rotating, and it ties the Jacobi lineage the corpus carries.
